headline: The First American HBM Plant Won't Make a Single Wafer — and Won't Ship Until 2029 | Manufacturing Mag
summary_text: SK hynix broke ground in West Lafayette on a $4B+ HBM facility that fabricates nothing, ships its first part in Q3 2029, and — under current CBP precedent — likely still counts as Korean-origin. A look at what $1.2 billion in public money actually bought. ... SK hynix broke ground on August 27, 2026 at Purdue Research Park in West Lafayette, Indiana, on what the company describes as the first HBM advanced packaging facility in the United States. The topline number is more than $4 billion — 5.52 trillion won. The site is 540,000 square meters of land owned by Purdue University. Indiana Governor Mike Braun attended. CEO Kwak Noh-Jung told CNBC the site would be a key memory production base in America by 2030. ... Two facts from that same announcement belong directly alongside the framing. The plant will not fabricate a wafer. And the first high-bandwidth memory stack packaged in Indiana is currently scheduled for the third quarter of 2029. ... - Scope: back-end only. Advanced DRAM wafers are produced in South Korea and shipped to Indiana for stacking, advanced packaging, and test before finished HBM goes to US customers. There is no front-end wafer fab in the plan. ... - Timeline: cleanroom completion targeted October 2028; mass production targeted Q3 2029. TrendForce reports the launch product is HBM4E. ... The NIST CHIPS program page for this award still states that mass production is expected to begin in the second half of 2028. At its own groundbreaking, SK hynix said Q3 2029. ... In ruling N326981, US Customs and Border Protection considered 12-inch wafers front-end fabbed in South Korea, back-end packaged in China or Taiwan, and finally tested in China. CBP held that the chips "do not undergo a substantial transformation as a result of the subsequent processing... They retain their identity with a predetermined end use." Country of origin remained South Korea, because front-end manufacturing is what imparts the essence to the integrated circuit. ... Applied to Indiana, that precedent points at an uncomfortable conclusion: HBM stacked and packaged in West Lafayette from Korean-fabbed wafers plausibly remains Korean-origin for marking and for Section 232 purposes. ... . An older CBP ruling, HQ 732357 from 1990, did find that converting wafers into packaged ICs was a substantial transformation. The modern line of rulings runs the other way for front-end/back-end splits, but the older holding exists. And SK hynix has not published an origin opinion for the Indiana output. What can ... Section 232 phase-two positioning. A 25% ad valorem tariff on a narrowly defined set of advanced computing chips and certain derivative products took effect January 15, 2026 (White & Case has the scope and exclusions). Analysts including ITIF expect a phase two that raises rates and adds an offset program rewarding firms investing in US semiconductor production. That offset — credit for having built here — is the most plausible mechanism by which Indiana pays off on trade policy. It rewards the capex, not the country-of-origin outcome. ... The public contribution is substantial relative to a back-end scope. Federal support runs to $458 million in CHIPS direct funding, up to $500 million in loans, and $8 million for workforce initiatives, as documented by NIST and reported by the Indianapolis Business Journal. ... Set the non-loan support against the announced headcount and the arithmetic is roughly $1.23 billion — $458M federal direct, up to $712M state, ~$60M in Purdue land and services — against about 1,000 direct jobs. That is on the order of $1.2 million per direct job before counting the $500 million loan facility. Indiana's share alone, at up to $772 million including the Purdue contribution, works out to roughly $772,000 per direct job. ... Those are high but not unheard-of numbers for a semiconductor project, and the ancillary case — an anchor tenant, a Purdue research relationship with access to the Birck Nanotechnology Center, a supplier cluster — is legitimate. But the state bought a back-end facility, not a fab, and the distinction should be visible in how the deal is evaluated in 2029. The jobs are packaging, test, and facilities jobs. The wafer capability stays in Korea. ... The most awkward feature of this project is its own CEO's demand outlook. Kwak has said there are no clear signs of a downturn, that memory supply stays tight through the end of 2030, and that 2027 will bring the most severe supply crunch the industry has ever seen. He expects supply and demand to balance after 2030. ... Indiana starts mass production in Q3 2029. On the company's own guidance, that is the tail end of the shortage — capacity arriving as the crisis resolves rather than while it bites. The 2027 crunch will be fought and settled with existing capacity. ... This is not unique to SK hynix. As StorageReview documents, essentially no announced new memory capacity lands before 2028 anywhere. SK hynix's Y2 DRAM fab breaks ground in July 2027 with cleanroom completion in June 2029. M17 NAND breaks ground February 2027 with first cleanroom December 2028. The industry committed billions on a horizon that does nothing for the near term, which is one reason ITIF cites a roughly 90% RAM price surge in Q1 2026. ... Micron's approach highlights the sequencing question. Its HBM advanced packaging is in Singapore, where construction started in January 2025, and elsewhere in Asia. Micron has said it will add HBM packaging in Virginia only after it builds sufficient US DRAM wafer scale at Boise — front end first, back end after. SK hynix is doing the reverse. No US front-end HBM DRAM wafer source exists at volume today, and this project does not create one. ... SK hynix's public roadmap puts HBM4 in 2026, HBM4E across 2026–2028, and HBM5/HBM5E in the 2029–2031 window. Indiana begins HBM4E mass production in Q3 2029 — opening on a generation the roadmap is already succeeding. ... For a back-end line, that is a tooling question, not just a marketing one. SK hynix said at Hot Chips 2026 that hybrid bonding will not be ready for HBM4E and is deferred to HBM5, as stack heights run into a 775-micron ceiling. A line specified and installed in 2028 for HBM4E is therefore a line specified around the pre-hybrid-bonding process — and one that may face a re-tool close to the start of its useful life, on a facility whose subsidy commitments are pinned to job counts and production milestones. ... Treat 2027 as a procurement problem, not a policy one. On the supplier's own guidance the crunch peaks before any of this capacity exists. Long-term agreements and forward commitments signed now are the lever; a 2029 groundbreaking is not. ... Budget qualification lead time separately from capacity. A new packaging site is a new qualification. Parts from a first-run Indiana line in late 2029 are not drop-in substitutes for qualified Korean-packaged parts on day one, and the qualification calendar should be modeled as its own line item. ... Route "domestically packaged" claims to trade compliance, not to supply security. Given N326981 and N336272, ask suppliers for the specific origin position and the ruling supporting it before relying on US packaging for tariff treatment, procurement preferences, or content requirements. And do not let a domestic back-end site substitute for a real answer about front-end concentration risk. ... What it is not is the start of American HBM manufacturing. It begins the US HBM supply chain at the wrong end, on a schedule that has already slipped a year against its own federal award documentation, opening on a memory generation its parent's roadmap is superseding, into a market its own CEO expects to be rebalancing. The wafer — the thing that under settled customs practice imparts the essence of the chip, and the thing that would actually constitute domestic capability — is still made in South Korea, and nothing announced this August changes that.

headline: America’s Pharmaceutical Reshoring Push Is Hitting a Wall – USA Business Times
summary_text: When President Biden signed the BIOSECURE Act provisions into law in late 2024 and the Trump administration doubled down with sweeping pharmaceutical tariffs earlier this year, the political consensus was unusually bipartisan: America could not afford to depend on foreign factories — primarily Chinese and Indian — for the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) that supply roughly 90 percent of its generic drug market. The message from Washington was unambiguous. Bring it home. ... Eighteen months later, the reshoring push is colliding with a wall of economic, regulatory, and workforce realities that neither party fully anticipated. Capital budgets are blowing past projections. FDA qualification timelines stretch years, not months. And the specialized chemical engineers needed to run API synthesis plants are, in the blunt assessment of one industry veteran, “nearly extinct in the American labor market.” ... The challenge begins with chemistry. Active pharmaceutical ingredients are not assembled like automobiles or semiconductors. They are synthesized through multi-step organic chemical reactions that require highly controlled environments, specialized reactors, and workers who understand both industrial chemistry and Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliance. That knowledge base migrated offshore over three decades, following cost incentives, and it does not simply snap back because tariffs change the math. ... ’s chief supply chain officer, Camille Hartley, addressed the complexity at the company’s investor day in Indianapolis last month. “We broke ground on our Lebanon, Indiana API campus in 2024. We told the market it would be online in 36 months. I am here to tell you honestly that 48 to 54 months is the more realistic timeline,” Hartley said. “FDA pre-approval inspections, equipment lead times for glass-lined reactors, and the simple reality of hiring 600 people who actually know what they’re doing — these are not problems money ... Lilly is hardly alone. Pfizer, Merck, and Abbott have all announced domestic API or fill-finish expansions since 2024. Across the industry, announced capital commitments total an estimated $38 billion through 2030, according to a recent analysis by the Reshoring Initiative. But announced commitments and completed, FDA-validated facilities are very different categories of achievement. ... Pfizer’s facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan — retooled at a cost of $1.1 billion to produce small-molecule APIs for cardiovascular and oncology drugs — received its FDA certification in March of this year, making it one of the first major reshored API sites to clear regulatory approval. CEO Albert Bourla called it “the most important manufacturing milestone for Pfizer since we scaled COVID-19 vaccine production in 2021.” ... But Pfizer’s Kalamazoo success is the exception. Several mid-size generic drugmakers, lacking the balance sheets of Big Pharma giants, are in genuine distress. Teva Pharmaceuticals, which had announced plans to shift API sourcing for five high-volume generics to a new facility in Knoxville, Tennessee, disclosed in a July 2026 SEC filing that the project is 22 months behind schedule and $340 million over its original budget. Mylan’s parent Viatris told investors in June it is reevaluating the scope of its West Virginia API project after construction bids came in 60 percent above projections. ... Washington’s toolkit has expanded considerably since 2023, but critics argue it remains insufficient and poorly coordinated. The current landscape of federal support includes: ... - The BARDA Strategic API Reserve Program, which offers long-term government purchase agreements for domestically produced APIs designated as critical medicines — but covers only 43 drug categories out of hundreds flagged as supply-chain risks. ... - Department of Defense Title III funding under the Defense Production Act, which has awarded approximately $2.7 billion to pharmaceutical manufacturing projects since 2024, with grants ranging from $40 million to $380 million per facility. ... - HHS’s American Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Tax Credit, enacted in the reconciliation package of early 2025, offering a 25 percent investment tax credit for qualified domestic API or finished dosage form construction — a provision that industry groups call helpful but say fails to address ongoing operational cost disadvantages. ... - The FDA’s newly created Office of Domestic Manufacturing Facilitation, which is supposed to provide expedited technical assistance to companies seeking GMP certification for new U.S. sites — but which, as of this summer, has a backlog of 71 pending facility consultations with a staff of 34. ... Senate HELP Committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-LA) acknowledged the capacity problem at a July hearing, noting that FDA’s inspection and certification pipeline “was not designed for a reshoring surge of this scale.” Cassidy has introduced legislation to appropriate $180 million for additional FDA manufacturing inspectors and fast-track certification resources, though the bill has not yet cleared the full Senate. ... Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has championed the tariff-driven reshoring agenda, pushed back against critics at a National Association of Manufacturers conference in Chicago last week. “Nobody said this was going to be easy or fast. But the alternative — leaving American patients dependent on Chinese chemical plants for their blood pressure medication and cancer drugs — is a national security failure we refuse to accept,” Lutnick said. “We are three years into a twenty-year project.” ... If capital is one constraint, human capital is the other — and in some ways the harder one to solve. The United States graduated roughly 9,200 chemical engineers in 2025, according to ASEE data, but demand from the semiconductor, battery, and pharmaceutical sectors is competing fiercely for that same talent pool. ... “Intel wants chemical engineers. TSMC’s Arizona fab wants chemical engineers. LG Energy Solution wants chemical engineers. Cincinnati State’s Process Technology program has added GMP coursework in partnership with Procter & Gamble’s health division. OSHA has also weighed in, issuing updated Process Safety Management guidance in April specifically addressing the chemical hazard profiles common in API synthesis — guidance that facilities directors describe as long overdue but that adds compliance complexity to an already demanding build-out environment. ... Industry analysts at Jefferies and William Blair now estimate that meaningful domestic API self-sufficiency — defined as U.S. facilities producing at least 40 percent of APIs consumed domestically — is unlikely before 2033 at the earliest, and possibly as late as 2037 under a slow-execution scenario. Their base case sits at 2034. ... That timeline carries real risk. A supply disruption from Chinese or Indian facilities — whether from geopolitical escalation, a natural disaster, or a major GMP failure — could hit American patients before the domestic infrastructure is ready to compensate. The FDA’s drug shortage database currently lists 213 active shortages, a number that has barely moved in two years despite the policy attention.

On a sprawling 87-acre campus outside Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, construction crews are working three shifts a day to finish what Eli Lilly executives are calling the company’s most consequential domestic investment in a generation. The $2.1 billion facility, slated to begin producing active pharmaceutical ingredients by the first quarter of 2027, is one of more than 60 major pharmaceutical manufacturing projects currently under construction across the United States — a surge of industrial activity that is fundamentally reshaping how America thinks about medical supply chain sovereignty. ... The boom is no accident. It is the product of converging pressures: lingering trauma from the COVID-19 pandemic’s drug shortage crisis, aggressive federal incentives embedded in the BIOSECURE Act of 2025, punishing new tariff regimes on Chinese and Indian API imports, and a growing bipartisan consensus in Washington that allowing foreign nations to control the supply of critical medicines is a national security liability that can no longer be tolerated. ... The pandemic shattered that complacency with brutal efficiency. Shortages of generic antibiotics, anesthetics, and critical care drugs exposed just how fragile those long supply chains had become. Then came the BIOSECURE Act, signed into law in March 2025, which barred federal health agencies from contracting with companies that source APIs from a list of designated Chinese biotechnology firms. The legislation didn’t just nudge the industry — it gave procurement officers and CFOs a hard deadline to restructure their supply chains or lose government business. ... Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that total announced domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing investment since January 2024 has exceeded $38 billion, with the bulk of that capital committed in the 18 months following the BIOSECURE Act’s passage. The figure dwarfs the semiconductor reshoring numbers from the CHIPS Act’s first two years and is drawing comparisons to the World War II-era industrial mobilization that converted civilian factories to war production. ... Not every state is positioned equally to capture this investment, and a fierce interstate competition has broken out that mirrors the semiconductor site wars of 2022 and 2023. North Carolina, which already hosts a dense cluster of contract drug manufacturers and biotech firms in the Research Triangle, has emerged as the early leader, landing more than $6 billion in announced projects over the past 18 months. ... Indiana, historically a pharmaceutical heartland thanks to Lilly’s century-long presence in Indianapolis, is close behind, with Governor Mike Braun’s administration deploying a targeted $400 million incentive package aimed specifically at API and sterile injectables manufacturing. The investment surge is generating a parallel labor crisis that industry executives describe as the single biggest operational constraint on the reshoring timeline. Pharmaceutical manufacturing requires a highly specialized workforce — process chemists, aseptic filling technicians, validation engineers, and quality assurance professionals who understand FDA’s stringent Good Manufacturing Practice regulations. That workforce takes years to develop and cannot be conjured quickly to meet a sudden burst of construction activity. ... Factory automation is increasingly seen as a partial answer. Companies like Pfizer and AbbVie are designing their new domestic facilities with higher automation ratios than equivalent plants built a decade ago, deploying continuous manufacturing systems, advanced robotics for sterile filling lines, and industrial IoT platforms that can monitor thousands of process variables in real time. These investments reduce headcount requirements per unit of output but raise the skill level of the workers who remain — intensifying, rather than eliminating, the talent competition. ... One of the less-examined stories inside the pharmaceutical reshoring surge is the dramatic expansion of domestic contract development and manufacturing organizations, known as CDMOs. Rather than every drug company building its own captive manufacturing infrastructure, a growing share of the new domestic capacity is being built by specialist manufacturers who will produce for multiple clients — a model that improves capital efficiency and allows smaller biotech firms to access Made-in-America supply chains without billion-dollar commitments. ... Private equity has taken notice: KKR, Blackstone, and Carlyle have all made significant CDMO acquisitions or investments in the past 18 months, betting that the structural shift toward domestic manufacturing is durable enough to justify premium valuations. ... Reshoring pharmaceutical manufacturing at this scale is not simply a matter of construction and hiring. The bond market is absorbing billions in new pharmaceutical manufacturing debt at favorable spreads. headline: America’s Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Comeback Hits a Critical Inflection Point – USA Business Times
summary_text: As of August 2026, the numbers tell a story of genuine momentum shadowed by persistent fragility. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration currently lists more than 200 active pharmaceutical ingredients — the chemical building blocks of everything from antibiotics to chemotherapy drugs — for which the United States has zero domestic manufacturing capacity. China and India together supply roughly 80 percent of the API inputs that American drug companies depend on. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed that dependence with brutal clarity. The fentanyl crisis added a national security dimension. And now, a combination of tariff pressure, bipartisan legislation, and raw corporate self-interest is reshaping where and how American medicine gets made. ... The policy architecture pushing pharmaceutical reshoring forward is more substantial than most outside the industry realize. The BIOSECURE Act, signed into law in early 2025, effectively prohibits federal agencies — including the Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs — from procuring pharmaceuticals manufactured in facilities with significant Chinese government equity stakes. That single measure sent shockwaves through a supply chain deeply entangled with firms like WuXi AppTec and Sinochem. The downstream effect: U.S. drug companies scrambling to qualify alternative suppliers and, in many cases, fund domestic alternatives. ... Simultaneously, the Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital has deployed more than $1.2 billion in low-interest loans and loan guarantees toward domestic API and finished-dose manufacturing projects since January 2025. The HHS’s Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response — ASPER — has signed long-term procurement contracts with domestic manufacturers of essential medicines, providing the kind of demand-side certainty that private investors have historically demanded before committing to capital-intensive factory builds. ... On Capitol Hill, the bipartisan American Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Security Act — co-sponsored by Senators Gary Peters of Michigan and Bill Hagerty of Tennessee — would create a domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing tax credit analogous to the CHIPS Act’s investment tax credit for semiconductor fabricators. The bill cleared the Senate Finance Committee in June with unusual bipartisan support and is expected to reach a floor vote before the end of the fiscal year. ... Beyond Eli Lilly’s Indiana megasite — which will produce GLP-1 receptor agonists including its blockbuster tirzepatide — a cluster of major players have announced or broken ground on significant domestic investments over the past eighteen months. ... - Pfizer has committed $3.1 billion to expand its McPherson, Kansas, sterile injectable facility, which will become one of the largest domestic finishing and packaging sites in the country by 2028. - Merck is investing $2.8 billion in a new biologics manufacturing campus in Durham, North Carolina, focused on oncology therapeutics. - Johnson & Johnson’s MedTech division is constructing a $1.6 billion orthopedic implant manufacturing hub in Warsaw, Indiana — a region already nicknamed “the orthopedic capital of the world.” - Civica Rx, the nonprofit generic drug consortium backed by major hospital systems, has its Petersburg, Virginia, facility now at full operational capacity, producing 15 essential generic injectable drugs that were previously sole-sourced from foreign manufacturers. - Phlow Corporation, in partnership with AMPAC Fine Chemicals, has expanded its Richmond, Virginia, API production campus and now supplies finished antibiotic ingredients to five major U.S. drug makers under long-term DoD contracts. ... The most acute is workforce. Pharmaceutical manufacturing requires a highly specialized labor pool — process chemists, sterile fill-finish operators, validation engineers, quality assurance specialists — and the U.S. pipeline of such workers was never rebuilt after the original offshore migration. Community colleges and technical schools are only now beginning to launch pharmaceutical manufacturing credential programs at scale, often in partnership with companies like Lilly and Pfizer. But the training cycle is long. A sterile fill-finish operator requires 18 to 24 months of specialized training before working independently on a production line. That timeline does not align cleanly with the urgency policymakers are projecting. ... Regulatory timeline is the second bottleneck. A new pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in the United States cannot begin commercial production until it has passed an FDA pre-approval inspection — a process that, even under the agency’s recently accelerated timelines, typically takes four to six years from groundbreaking to first validated batch. Factories announced today will not meaningfully relieve supply chain stress until the early 2030s. ... Cost remains a stubborn variable. Domestic API production costs run 40 to 60 percent higher than equivalent Chinese or Indian production, even accounting for current tariff levels on pharmaceutical imports. For branded drugs with robust margins, that differential is manageable. For generic manufacturers — who supply 90 percent of American prescriptions by volume — it can be the difference between a viable business ... The one development that could fundamentally alter the cost calculus is continuous manufacturing — an advanced production approach that replaces the traditional batch-by-batch pharmaceutical production model with an integrated, automated, end-to-end process. The FDA has been actively championing continuous manufacturing adoption since 2019, and recent advances in process analytical technology and industrial IoT sensor integration have made it far more commercially viable. ... Eli Lilly’s new Indiana facility is designed as a continuous manufacturing showcase from the ground up. So is Pfizer’s expanded Kansas site. The operational advantage is significant: continuous manufacturing requires roughly one-third the facility footprint of equivalent batch capacity, dramatically reduces labor inputs per unit produced, and can cut quality control cycle times from weeks to hours. In a domestic context — where labor costs are the primary competitive disadvantage — those reductions are transformative. ... Rockwell Automation, which is supplying the industrial control architecture for several of the new domestic pharma builds, projects that a fully automated continuous manufacturing line can reduce the labor cost differential between U.S. and offshore production by as much as 35 percentage points. “The factory of 2030 looks very different from the factory of 2010,” said Blake Moret, Rockwell’s chairman and CEO. “Automation doesn’t replace the reshoring argument — it enables it. It’s what makes the American wage structure survivable in a globally competitive market.” ... But the broader reshoring of generic drug API production — the supply chain layer that actually determines whether a hospital can fill a prescription for amoxicillin or furosemide during a crisis — remains deeply contingent on sustained federal procurement commitments, the passage of the pharmaceutical manufacturing tax credit, and continued tariff pressure on foreign competitors. Remove those policy pillars and the economic logic of domestic production weakens considerably. ... What is clear is that the political will, in both parties, is stronger than at any point in recent memory. The spectacle of American hospitals rationing chemotherapy drugs and saline bags during COVID-19 left a bipartisan mark on the congressional psyche that has not faded. Pharmaceutical manufacturing security now sits alongside semiconductor fabrication and shipbuilding on the short list of industrial capabilities that Washington has decided the United States cannot afford to source entirely from overseas.

The question in August 2026 is no longer whether America is serious about rebuilding its pharmaceutical supply chain. The question is whether it can actually do it in time. ... The forces reshaping American pharmaceutical manufacturing are neither simple nor singular. Trade policy, national security legislation, pandemic-era trauma, and a retooled incentive architecture have converged in ways that even optimists inside the industry did not fully anticipate. ... The BIOSECURE Act, which passed in a narrow Senate vote in March 2025 and was signed by President Trump shortly thereafter, effectively barred U.S. government contractors from sourcing APIs from a list of designated Chinese biotechnology firms — a list that has since grown to include 14 major suppliers. For companies like Pfizer and Abbott Laboratories, the legislation functionally forced a sourcing reckoning that internal procurement teams had been quietly delaying for years. ... At the same time, the expanded Section 232 tariffs on pharmaceutical precursor chemicals — implemented in tranches throughout 2025 — raised the landed cost of imported APIs sharply enough to alter the fundamental economics of offshore sourcing. For generics manufacturers, whose margins were already razor-thin, the math shifted almost overnight. ... The geography of America’s pharmaceutical manufacturing renaissance is telling. While legacy hubs like New Jersey and North Carolina remain important, the real construction boom is spreading into states that have aggressively competed for investment through tax incentives, streamlined permitting, and workforce development partnerships with community colleges. ... - Texas: Eli Lilly broke ground in April 2026 on a $4.1 billion API synthesis campus outside San Antonio, which the company says will eventually produce insulin analogues and GLP-1 compounds domestically. The speed of construction is creating friction with the regulatory apparatus designed to oversee it. The FDA’s inspection workforce has not expanded proportionally with the number of new domestic facilities seeking approval, creating a backlog that manufacturers say is adding six to twelve months to facility qualification timelines. ... FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary acknowledged the bottleneck in a July press briefing, announcing a pilot program to hire 340 additional facility inspectors by the end of fiscal year 2027 and to expand the use of remote regulatory assessments — a tool first deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic — for lower-risk manufacturing categories. ... OSHA, meanwhile, is navigating its own growing pains. The agency’s National Emphasis Program on pharmaceutical manufacturing, updated in early 2026, introduced stricter standards around solvent exposure, ergonomic hazards in high-speed packaging operations, and process safety management for high-potency API facilities. Not every pharmaceutical company has the capital or strategic appetite to own and operate API manufacturing facilities. For mid-sized biotechs, specialty pharma companies, and even some large generics manufacturers, the contract development and manufacturing organization model — wherein a third party owns and operates the facility while the brand company contracts for capacity — has become the preferred vehicle for reshoring exposure without full capital commitment. ... The Department of Health and Human Services released a list of 86 “essential medicines” in April 2026, the domestic production of which is now explicitly incentivized under the CHIPS-and-Science Act’s pharmaceutical manufacturing addendum. ... As cranes rise across San Antonio, Dayton, and the Research Triangle, and as workforce pipelines slowly ramp, the verdict on America’s pharmaceutical manufacturing revival remains unwritten. The capital is committed. The legislation is in place. The workforce programs are enrolling. What the country is discovering, at significant cost and with some urgency, is that rebuilding an industrial base hollowed out over thirty years is not a quarterly earnings story. It is a decade-long undertaking — and in August 2026, that decade is only just beginning.

headline: Middle-market employers are finally warming to pooled retirement plans | Insurance Business
summary_text: Middle-market employers have long faced a disproportionate share of retirement plan complexity, spending management time and absorbing fiduciary risk that larger competitors can spread across dedicated internal teams. ... Mike Ziccardi, Executive Vice President of CBIZ's Retirement & Investment Solutions Practice, has been speaking to Insurance Business America about the Pooled Employer Plan (PEP) landscape as his firm brings a new product to market. ... "Managing a retirement plan has become increasingly complex," he said. "Employers are expected to navigate evolving regulations, oversee investments, manage vendors, and absorb fiduciary risk – all while controlling costs. A PEP lets multiple employers share one professionally managed 401(k) plan, greatly reducing administrative burden and fiduciary responsibility." ... Launched last month, the CBIZ Retirement Advantage PEP consolidates what has historically been a patchwork of individual plan structures into a single, institutionally managed framework. ... PEPs have been available since 2021, enabled by the SECURE Act of 2019, but middle-market uptake has been measured. Ziccardi says the pattern is familiar. ... "Like many innovations across the employee benefits landscape, adoption tends to start in the large-market segment before working its way downstream," he said. "Many middle-market employers have preferred to take a wait-and-see approach, allowing early adopters to test the model before making a change themselves." ... "We are beginning to see the market thaw," Ziccardi said. "As PEPs establish a longer track record and employers become more comfortable with the structure, interest is increasing. The growth is likely to be gradual rather than sudden, but momentum is clearly building." ... According to the US Department of Labor's 2025 Pooled Employer Plan Bulletin, PEP adoption has continued to accelerate since the SECURE Act's passage, with hundreds of plans now registered across the country. ... For many business owners, the most compelling aspect of a PEP is not potential cost savings, but the transfer of fiduciary responsibility. Ziccardi says the broader advisory conversation has shifted well beyond that single issue. ... "The conversation has evolved well beyond investments," he said. "Historically, many employers viewed retirement plan advisors primarily through the lens of investment oversight. Today, fiduciary risk management, governance, cybersecurity, participant outcomes, fee reasonableness, and operational compliance are often taking center stage." ... As litigation and regulatory scrutiny increase, Ziccardi says employers are becoming more selective. ... "We're seeing a gradual shift away from investment generalists toward firms that can help navigate the increasingly complex fiduciary and regulatory environment surrounding workplace retirement plans." ... When employers do move to a PEP structure, Ziccardi urges careful vetting of the pooled plan provider (PPP) – the named fiduciary responsible for selecting, monitoring, and replacing key service providers within the arrangement. ... "A key red flag is when a PPP occupies multiple roles within the arrangement," he said. "For example, if the PPP is also serving as the advisor or recordkeeper, employers should carefully evaluate how potential conflicts of interest are being managed. After all, effective oversight requires independence, and employers should understand who is truly holding service providers accountable." ... Retirement plan quality has become a key differentiator in talent acquisition, and Ziccardi says the way middle-market employers think about their 401(k) has fundamentally changed. For brokers who advise business clients on how pooled retirement structures are reshaping employee benefits strategies, the shift in employer mindset is significant. ... "Leading middle-market employers no longer view their retirement plan in isolation," Ziccardi said. "Instead, it's becoming an integrated component of a broader benefits, financial wellness, and total rewards strategy. What's changed is that technology, automation, AI, and data integration capabilities have made personalization accessible to organizations of virtually any size." ... "Consumers receive personalized recommendations everywhere else in their lives, whether through streaming platforms, online shopping, or social media," he said. "Increasingly, they expect their benefits experience to feel just as relevant and personalized. As a result, employers are focusing less on simply offering a plan and more on creating an experience that improves engagement, financial confidence, and retirement readiness." ... "Many advisors lead with cost savings, but that can oversimplify the value proposition," he said. "The idea of pooling employers together to create economies of scale has existed for years in the health and welfare space, so it's natural for cost to be part of the conversation. However, cost should not be the primary lens through which a PEP is evaluated." ... The better questions, he argues, go deeper. "The more important considerations are whether the PEP meaningfully reduces fiduciary burden, simplifies administration for HR and payroll teams, and ultimately, improves participant outcomes. Fee savings may certainly be part of the equation, but employers should also evaluate the quality of participant support, technology capabilities, financial wellness resources, and overall employee experience." ... Ziccardi is also clear-eyed about the structural limits of the model. He doesn’t believe PEPs will become the default structure anytime soon, but he does think they will experience significant growth in certain segments of the market. ... “For PEPs to become truly mainstream, employers will need greater awareness of the fiduciary and administrative benefits, continued proof of successful outcomes, and more confidence that they can achieve those benefits without sacrificing the flexibility that matters most to their organization,” he said. ... CBIZ's integrated model of combining retirement consulting with employee benefits, insurance, payroll, and advisory services, is designed to address exactly that concern as the intersection of retirement, insurance and professional services is increasingly where the most meaningful workforce strategy conversations are happening.

headline: New paid leave bill puts private insurance at the center | Insurance Business
summary_text: A bipartisan paid leave bill moving through Congress contains a provision absent from recent major federal paid leave proposals: a mandate that states partner with private entities to administer benefits. That structural detail is the part worth watching for benefits brokers tracking the PFML market. ... The Senate bill, S.5017, was introduced on July 16, by Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York and John Boozman of Arkansas, as the companion to a House bill filed in April 2025 by Reps. Stephanie Bice of Oklahoma and Chrissy Houlahan of Pennsylvania. The Albany Times Union reported Gillibrand's comments on the legislation. Both bills remain in committee. ... The bill does not create a national paid family and medical leave (PFML) program. It establishes a three-year grant program administered by the Department of Labor, with competitive awards of $1.5 million to $7 million per state. To qualify, a state must use a public-private partnership model and offer at least six weeks of leave tied to at least one qualifying reason under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). ... The bill defines a qualifying partnership as a state arrangement with at least one private entity, such as an insurance company handling administrative functions, the benefit application process, or claims. States may also allow employers to self-administer. That language gives insurers and group benefits carriers a defined role in any state that receives a federal grant. ... The American Council of Life Insurers (ACLI) has already signaled support for the bill. In a statement, it noted that the private sector has delivered paid leave benefits at scale for nearly a century, with approximately 67 million Americans covered by employer-based short-term disability insurance. Life insurers and employers paid out $8.6 billion in paid leave benefits in 2024, according to the ACLI. ... Twenty-seven states currently have no paid family leave program of any kind, according to the Boozman-Gillibrand press release. If those states build programs under this framework, the addressable market for insured PFML products would expand. The same pattern is already visible at the state level: Maryland opened private paid-leave filings in June, setting a September 30 cutoff for carriers to file forms and rates for private plans employers can buy in place of the state-run program. ... The bill includes a second title: the Interstate Paid Leave Action Network, or I-PLAN. It creates a voluntary multi-state working group with common definitions, administrative standards, and a shared claims-processing technology framework. Participating states receive annual conforming grants of $1.5 million to $8 million. ... For brokers advising multi-state employers, the I-PLAN component addresses a problem that has grown as PFML programs expand. There are now 16 jurisdictions with active mandatory PFML programs, each running on its own rules and timelines. When those programs stack against federal FMLA obligations and employer-sponsored short-term disability plans, the compliance gaps are material. ... A shared standard across even a handful of participating states would cut that burden. The group voluntary benefits and disability markets have been absorbing the cost of that fragmentation for years. ... Not all policy observers support the private-entity requirement. Jane Waldfogel, a professor at Columbia University School of Social Work, told the Times Union that most paid leave programs historically use a public delivery model. She said requiring private partners risks diverting funds to insurance profits and added the requirement was likely a legislative compromise. ... Sharita Gruberg, vice president for economic justice at the National Partnership for Women and Families in Washington, raised a separate concern. She said the bill does not actually establish a paid leave program and may set a lower bar for future national policy. Her preferred legislation, the Family and Medical Insurance Leave (FAMILY) Act, would establish a federal program covering all workers regardless of employer size. ... The bills' prospects are uncertain. Both are in committee, and paid leave legislation has stalled in Congress repeatedly over the past decade. Francine Blau, a professor of industrial and labor relations at Cornell University, told the Times Union she believes the bill has promise, citing its bipartisan structure. ... For carriers and brokers in the group benefits space, the bill's outcome maps to a clear fork. Passage expands the insured PFML market in 27 states that currently have nothing. Failure leaves the market where it is: growing state by state, on terms that vary widely in whether private plan alternatives are permitted at all.

summary_text: Independent agency owners weighing a sale are working with a smaller list of buyers than they were two years ago, even as the number of agencies looking for an exit keeps growing. ... That widening gap is the setting for American Growth Insurance's (AGI) acquisition of Baltimore's Heller-Kowitz Insurance Advisors, the first deal in a strategy AGI says will build a network of operator-led agencies starting in the Mid-Atlantic. ... The buyer side of that equation has been thinning for four straight years. The number of unique acquirers active in agency M&A fell from 104 in 2024 to 95 in 2025, according to OPTIS Partners, even as the firm estimates roughly 30,000 independent agencies with revenues below $1.25 million remain in operation, most without a succession plan in place. ... Overall deal volume tells a similar story. OPTIS Partners data puts the trailing 12-month total at 646 agency transactions, the lowest rolling count since early 2019, even though private equity-backed and hybrid buyers still accounted for 75% of those deals and 80% of everything closed in the second quarter of 2026 alone. Of the 68 unique buyers active in the first half of 2026, 37 were private equity-backed, including six making their first-ever agency acquisition, a group AGI now joins as established consolidators slow their pace. ... Heller-Kowitz, founded in ... 14 by Steve Heller and Brian Kowitz, holds Reagan Consulting Best Practices agency status and writes personal lines, commercial lines, employee benefits and life insurance. Kowitz said the agency had drawn acquisition interest for years, and that most offers looked interchangeable. ... He said AGI's structure stood out from that pattern. "AGI's approach stood apart. We recognized a unique opportunity to combine operational excellence with purposeful leadership; creating a long-term strategy that prioritizes our clients' well-being while leveraging state-of-the-art technology and AI-driven innovation," Kowitz said. "We believe this partnership positions us to deliver even greater value, efficiency, and service for our clients for years to come." ... He added, "We believe the most successful ... combine innovative technology with talented, engaged people. By ... technology to streamline routine processes, provide ... insights, and improve service delivery, we enable our ... to spend more time focused on clients, ... What that looks like in practice, according to AGI, is a model built before this deal rather than around it. The company said it spent roughly a year developing and testing its technology with 10 agencies, and has said that pilot lifted average agency profitability by more than 50% through revenue and productivity gains. AGI has also described a governance structure in which partner firms retain a seat in shaping strategy and technology decisions. ... AGI's case rests partly on a scale gap it says smaller agencies can't close alone. Citing MarshBerry data, the company has said the 50 largest US brokers account for 96% of industry revenue, leaving independent firms with comparatively limited resources to compete on technology or growth without outside capital. ... AGI CEO Brian Morgan pointed to that combination of operator experience and shared technology as the pitch to agencies still deciding whether to sell. ... "We believe the future of insurance will be built by combining great operators with great technology," Morgan said. "Heller-Kowitz is exactly the kind of agency we want in our network: strong client relationships, deep expertise, and a reputation for service. The real value is becoming an AI-native company, not just using AI point solutions." ... ## Owners in the same region are watching multiple buyers Heller-Kowitz is not the only Mid-Atlantic agency finding a new home this year. Ensurise LLC, a Greater Washington advisory firm, merged with WSMT Insurance, a Maryland personal and commercial lines agency, in March 2026, adding to a platform Ensurise has grown through partnership deals since 2014. ... That regional activity sits inside a wider national count of 241 announced US brokerage deals through the end of May 2026, down 5.1% from the same point a year earlier, with private capital-backed buyers responsible for 70.5% of that total, according to MarshBerry. For an owner in the region, that means AGI is one option among several active buyers, not the only one making a case. ... With its first acquisition complete, AGI said it plans to continue adding brokerage operators seeking greater scale, automation and access to a wider carrier network, while maintaining the client relationships that drive each acquired agency's business. ... Those plans, like the figures behind AGI's pilot program, remain the company's own account of what comes next. Whether that pitch holds up against a shrinking field of buyers and an even larger field of agencies weighing their own exit will be the question worth watching as AGI's next deals close.

While the market remains active, transactions activity continues to trail last year’s pace. With broader macro uncertainty in 2026 – which includes elevated borrowing costs, continued geopolitical volatility, and now energy price pressure – there is a more cautious dealmaking environment, particularly for buyers that rely heavily on leverage. ... Strategically, the market continues to shift toward quality over quantity. Buyers are prioritizing niche expertise, organic growth potential, and operational fit, while also emphasizing integration and value creation post-close. At the same time, macro pressures – higher interest rates, slower organic growth, and tighter financing – are tempering large, highly leveraged deals. High-quality firms with strong organic growth, specialty capabilities, and durable margins should continue to command strong interest and elevated valuations, while weaker or more rate-dependent firms may face a tougher valuation environment. headline: Egypt Explores Major Data Centre and AI Hub Project With Heka Data, US Consortium - TechAfrica News
summary_text: # Egypt Explores Major Data Centre and AI Hub Project With Heka Data, US Consortium September 4, 2026 Author: Joyce Onyeagoro The discussions covered the company’s plans to establish an integrated major data center and AI hub in Egypt, capitalizing on the country’s competitive advantages to position Egypt as a regional and global hub for data centers, cloud computing, and digital services. Minister of Communications and Information Technology Raafat Hendy has met with a delegation from data center developer Heka Data and a U.S. consortium of data center developers, led by Chairman of Heka Data Ahmed El-Hefny. The discussions covered the company’s plans to establish an integrated major data center and AI hub in Egypt, capitalizing on the country’s competitive advantages to position Egypt as a regional and global hub for data centers, cloud computing, and digital services. ... The meeting was attended by Executive President of the National Telecom Regulatory Authority (NTRA) Mohamed Shamroukh, CEO of the Information Technology Industry Development Agency (ITIDA) Ahmed Elzaher, Head of the Central Department for Resources and Technical Assistance and Acting Head of the Central Department for Technological Projects and Outsourcing at the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) Saad Roshdy, along with senior officials from MCIT, NTRA, and Telecom Egypt. ... The meeting explored opportunities to collaborate on the project, leveraging Egypt’s strategic location, advanced digital infrastructure, fiber-optic networks, and subsea cable system connecting the country to regions around the world, along with its growing pool of specialized ICT talent. ... The ICT Minister said Egypt remains committed to building international partnerships with companies and institutions specializing in data center development and digital infrastructure, drawing on global expertise and technology to strengthen its position as a regional data center hub. The government, he said, welcomes strategic investments that support the transfer and local development of emerging technologies and help build an integrated data center and AI ecosystem serving Egyptian, regional, and international markets. Expanding this industry, he added, is a key driver of Egypt’s economic competitiveness and a pathway to attracting further technology investment. ... Hendy noted that the rapid advancement of AI is driving growing demand for advanced digital infrastructure, particularly high-performance data centers. He explained that Egypt is developing an integrated ecosystem designed to accommodate this growth, create an enabling environment for advanced digital services, and strengthen the country’s capacity to host and process data and serve businesses and institutions in Egypt and across the region. ... For their part, the Heka Data delegation and the U.S. consortium presented their vision for the project and highlighted the potential of the Egyptian market, which they described as one of the region’s most promising markets. They further expressed their interest in deepening cooperation with the Egyptian government and moving forward with the necessary studies and procedures to advance the project. ... The meeting addressed the project’s initial scope, scale, and implementation phases, along with the investment and technology opportunities it could offer, its potential to generate new jobs, and its role in supporting the growth of cloud computing, AI, and digital services in Egypt and the region. The discussions also examined measures to establish an enabling environment for the project and streamline the necessary procedures in coordination with the relevant authorities. ... The meeting also highlighted the government’s efforts to develop digital infrastructure and create a supportive environment for the expansion of the data center industry, a key pillar of the digital economy and a major driver of the growth of cloud computing, AI, and digital services. ... In addition, the discussion underscored the importance of integrating digital infrastructure with the power supply needed to operate data centers, ensuring reliable and efficient operations, particularly as global demand for data center services continues to grow rapidly, driven by the expansion of cloud computing and AI applications.

headline: Sovereign Cloud $80B in 2026: MEA Grows Fastest at 89%
summary_text: Gartner forecasts worldwide sovereign cloud IaaS spending to reach $80 billion in 2026, up 35.6% from 2025, with the Middle East and Africa projected to grow 89% — the fastest of any region. A wave of national frameworks in Nigeria, South Africa and Mauritania in mid-2026 is turning data-localization policy into a regional infrastructure market, and Algeria’s own hosting providers sit inside that opening. ... Quick Take: The 89% MEA growth figure is a countdown for Algerian providers. Governments and regulated industries — not enterprises — are the buyers, so the winning move is to secure a public-sector or energy-sector anchor tenant, build a certification story that mirrors Nigeria’s NDIAF, and compete on provable control (keys, operators, jurisdiction) rather than server location. Providers that are certification-ready when regulated buyers start localizing will capture the spend; those that wait will watch hyperscaler “sovereign” sub-brands take it first. ... Sovereign cloud has spent two years as a European boardroom story — Gaia-X, the Cloud Act, hyperscaler “EU-only” pledges. In 2026, the fastest growth is happening somewhere else entirely. According to Gartner’s February 2026 forecast, reported by w.media, worldwide sovereign cloud infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) spending will total $80 billion in 2026, a 35.6% increase over 2025 — and the Middle East and Africa (MEA) region is projected to record the highest growth of any region at 89%, ahead of Mature Asia/Pacific (87%) and Europe (83%). ... That figure is not a market curiosity. It is a policy signal. Gartner attributes the surge to “geopatriation” — the movement of workloads back onto locally controlled infrastructure — and expects sovereign cloud spending to shift roughly 20% of current workloads from global to local cloud providers, per the same w.media report of Gartner’s data. Crucially, Gartner names governments as the main buyers, “followed by regulated industries and critical infrastructure organizations, such as energy and utilities and telecommunications.” That buyer profile is the reason MEA is moving so fast: this is state-driven demand, not enterprise experimentation. ... In August 2026, Nigeria’s National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) unveiled the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative (NSCI), signing three regulatory instruments — the National Cloud Computing Guideline, the National Cloud Technical Guideline, and the National Digital Infrastructure Assurance Framework (NDIAF). NITDA explicitly framed the initiative as positioning Nigeria as “a regional hub for cloud services, data centres, artificial intelligence infrastructure, sovereign computing and other critical digital infrastructure”, and set an October 2026 target to operationalize a national platform for onboarding, certifying and regulating cloud providers operating in the country. The agency also cited a hard cost of inaction: cybercrime cost Nigeria more than $3 billion between 2019 and 2025, the kind of number that turns “sovereignty” from a slogan into a budget line. ... Nigeria was not alone. summary_text: North Africa’s 5G Boom Faces Performance Declines After Strong Launches - TechAfrica News # North Africa’s 5G Boom Faces Performance Declines After Strong Launches August 7, 2026 Author: Kay-Lyne Wolfenden Tunisia and Egypt launched 5G in 2025, followed later that year by Morocco and Algeria, with differences in spectrum allocation and deployment strategies contributing to contrasting performance trends. North Africa’s 5G rollout delivered significant initial speed gains across the region, but network performance varied considerably during the six months following commercial launches, according to Ookla’s Speedtest data. Tunisia and Egypt launched 5G in 2025, followed later that year by Morocco and Algeria, with differences in spectrum allocation and deployment strategies contributing to contrasting performance trends. ... All four markets adopted 5G Non-Standalone (NSA) architecture, although their approaches differed. Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria deployed dedicated 3.5 GHz mid-band spectrum, while Egypt refarmed existing 2.6 GHz TDD spectrum. Tunisia placed particular emphasis on 5G Fixed Wireless Access (FWA), while Morocco introduced coverage obligations and Algeria adopted a phased rollout across its provinces. ... The spectrum choices had a direct impact on initial 5G speeds. Algeria recorded a median 5G download speed of 484.6 Mbps on launch day, nearly 19 times its 4G baseline, while Tunisia reached 223.1 Mbps, more than nine times its 4G speed. Morocco recorded 261.7 Mbps, almost six times its 4G baseline, while Egypt reached 110.5 Mbps, a 3.5-fold improvement. Egypt recorded the most stable performance, ending the six-month period at 89 Mbps after fluctuations within a relatively narrow range. ... The report also found that the benefits of 5G did not necessarily translate into sustained improvements in overall network performance. Algeria was the exception, with aggregate speeds rising 49% from 30.6 Mbps before launch to 45.6 Mbps in the sixth month, alongside a 7% improvement in 4G performance. ... In Egypt, the combined 4G and 5G median initially rose by 60% during the launch month but eventually declined to 34.77 Mbps, below its pre-launch baseline of 37.68 Mbps. Morocco recorded a 113% launch-month increase before falling to 44.59 Mbps by the sixth month, while Tunisia’s combined performance declined from a launch peak of 70.65 Mbps to 31.73 Mbps. Both Morocco and Tunisia also recorded declines in 4G performance during the period. ... Under the updated compliance structure, securing a CED license is no longer optional—it is an absolute prerequisite for market participation. According to the CA’s public notice, the license is mandatory for firms seeking to: ... - Import communications equipment on a wholesale basis into the Kenyan market. - Have their specific equipment models type-approved by the Authority. - Clear commercial shipments through the government’s centralized TradeNet customs system. ... The regulatory net is cast wide. Equipment subjected to the new type-approval and licensing framework includes mobile cellular devices across 2G to 5G spectrums, Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) hardware, complex radio communication infrastructure including microwave and satellite transmitters, and standard data equipment such as routers and network switches. ... One of the most consequential elements of the CA’s directive is its retroactive application to established industry players. summary_text: Epson has officially launched its SurePress digital label press in South Africa, marking the first time the model is operating on the African continent and signalling a significant expansion of advanced digital label printing capability into the region. The facility forms part of Epson’s broader strategy to strengthen local skills development and allow customers to adopt new print applications with confidence. ... Gareth Jay, Regional Sales Director for Africa at Epson, says the introduction of SurePress reflects a clear shift in market demand. “There is a marked increase in demand for short-run and personalised output across the print sector, and label production is no exception. SurePress enables customers to respond to that demand with greater flexibility, consistency and control, while maintaining high print quality across a wider range of substrates. ... “Crucially, it delivers true commercial viability for short runs, allowing local businesses to break away from massive volume requirements that spike upfront costs and limit operational flexibility. Instead of relying on rigid, overseas supply chains just to make a print run viable, providers can now produce high-quality labels right here in South Africa, matching demand exactly as it happens, he continues. ... Altron Document Solutions, Head of Production Systems, Keith Knott said the partnership reflects a shared commitment to enabling practical innovation for South African customers. ... “Our partnership with Epson allows us to bring proven technology into the market, backed by our 60-year local legacy and a shared commitment to reliability. The SurePress platform is positioned to support printers looking to expand into label production or scale existing capabilities, particularly in environments where flexibility and efficiency are increasingly critical. ... Key capabilities include enhanced water-based inks designed to improve substrate versatility, increased drying efficiency for improved productivity on film materials, and an expanded colour gamut for high-quality output. Improved automated maintenance functions also support more efficient short-run production. ... At the same time, Epson has ensured that sustainability remains at the core of the product design. Grounded in its Sho-Sho-Sei philosophy, Epson designed the SurePress model to be compact, efficient and precise, reducing energy use and material waste while improving operational efficiency. The company continues to align product development with practical sustainability outcomes for industrial print environments. ... The availability of SurePress in South Africa forms part of Epson’s broader ambition to deepen its footprint across Africa, where the company operates in 11 countries and continues to invest in technology, partnerships and local capability development.

He said the mismatch was what forced airlines to absorb significant losses. ... On the issue of fuel prices, he said it represented another significant burden that airlines pass to consumers. headline: Dangote vessel acquisition plan exposes Nigeria’s shipping capacity gap-Industry expert - Businessday NG
summary_text: Dangote Group’s plan to acquire vessels to move its products across West and Central Africa has exposed Nigeria’s failure to build enough indigenous shipping capacity, according to experts. Ladi Olubowale, an indigenous shipowner and former president of the African Shipowners Association, said Dangote was justified in seeking its own vessels because cargo owners cannot afford to wait for Nigerian shipowners to develop the capacity to serve their needs. But he said the group’s large cargo base could instead be used to help build a stronger Nigerian-owned fleet through long-term contracts with qualified indigenous operators. “There is nothing inherently wrong with the Dangote Group owning vessels,” Olubowale said at an interaction on ... He said Dangote could commit part of its cargo requirements to Nigerian shipowners through medium- and long-term contracts of affreightment, time charters and other bankable cargo commitments. The comments come after BusinessDay reported that the Dangote Group plans to acquire vessels due to limited shipping capacity in Nigeria and the high cost of moving its products by road. Olubowale said the problem was not that Dangote was using foreign shipping capacity, but that Nigerian operators had failed to provide vessels of the size and specification required by major cargo owners. “When Nigerian operators do not possess vessels of the appropriate size, specification and operational capability required by major cargo owners, commerce will not wait for us. The cargo will move. And somebody else’s ships will carry it,” he said. ... Olubowale, who is the managing director of Seamate Group, said the immediate priority for Nigeria should therefore be to match its cargo with vessels and financing, rather than encouraging ship acquisition without a clear commercial market. “Shipping is attached to trade,” he said. “Before acquiring a vessel, a serious shipowner must understand the cargo, its volume, the route, frequency, vessel specification, charter structure and duration of the commercial opportunity.” ... Nigeria already has cargo capable of supporting a larger indigenous fleet, he said, pointing to oil and gas, agriculture, cement, fertiliser and refined petroleum products. The Dangote Group’s expanding industrial operations, particularly the refinery, could provide a substantial cargo base for Nigerian-controlled vessels and help turn the country into a regional shipping hub, he said. But that would require cargo owners, shipowners, the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency, financial institutions, development finance institutions, Afreximbank, insurers and international technical partners to jointly map the country’s maritime cargo requirements. ... The exercise should establish the volumes of crude, refined petroleum products, fertiliser, cement and dry bulk cargo available over five, 10 and 15 years, as well as the routes and vessel types required to move them, Olubowale said. “Once we understand the trade, we can determine the fleet. Not the other way around,” he said. ... He said the exercise could identify the Aframax tankers, product tankers, bulk carriers, coastal vessels and other specialised assets required by Nigerian cargo owners, after which qualified shipowners could be matched with specific cargo opportunities. Olubowale also argued that the $700m Cabotage Vessel Financing Fund should be assessed against its ability to create commercially sustainable vessels rather than simply the number of shipowners that receive financing. “The real measure should be: How many commercially sustainable Nigerian-controlled vessels did the fund create? How much Nigerian cargo did those vessels capture?” he said. He said a shipowner approaching a bank with a firm, multi-year cargo contract would present a stronger financing proposition than one seeking money to buy a vessel without secured cargo. “The cargo becomes the foundation of the financing,” he said. “The contract gives visibility to future earnings. The vessel becomes connected to an identifiable trade.” Olubowale warned that financing vessels without first securing cargo could leave shipowners with expensive assets but no sustainable business. “Nigeria needs the opposite: Identify the cargo. Secure the trade. Structure the financing. Acquire the appropriate vessel,” he said. ... He said the economic cost of Nigeria’s shipping capacity gap extends beyond freight payments, as foreign-controlled vessels also capture charter revenues, technical management, insurance, ship-management, maintenance and employment opportunities. “Every time Nigerian cargo is transported by foreign-controlled shipping capacity because suitable indigenous capacity does not exist, freight payments leave the economy,” he said. “Government’s responsibility is to create the regulatory, financial and commercial environment that allows competent indigenous operators to thrive.” Bethel Olujobi is the Trade Correspondent at BusinessDay. He brings scarce insight into Nigeria's maritime policies and the changing currents of global commerce defining the country's position in international trade. Before this, he reported on foreign relations, migration and sports for BusinessDay. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Mass Communication, and is an alumni of the CNN Academy and the Financial Times News School. He is certified by Reuters and Google. He is based in Lagos, Nigeria. headline: Nigeria’s Cargo Corridor: How Layered Taxes, Offshore Insurance Are Quietly Eroding Air Freight Competitiveness – Independent Newspaper Nigeria
summary_text: 1, 2026 ... of Nigerian produce ... for Europe now ... tax code, a fragmented insurance market and a currency in flux; as industry data suggests the toll is getting heavier, not lighter. ... Follow one consignment of fresh produce from a Lagos warehouse to a European tarmac, and the cost stack tells its own story. Before the goods even reach the aircraft, they pass through cargo registration fees, export charges, courier and tarmac levies, landing charges and trans-shipment costs, a sequence airline operators say has ballooned into one of the most burdensome fee regimes in West Africa. Professor Obiora Okonkwo, Chairman of United Nigeria Airlines and spokesman for the Airline Operators of Nigeria (AON), has put a number on the ticketing side of that burden: airlines are charged around 18 separate taxes on a single ticket, with roughly 70 per cent of the fare flowing to government agencies rather than the carrier. ... Cargo shippers face an equivalent maze of registration, extension and demurrage charges layered by regulators including the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA). ... The financial strain is visible in the results of Nigeria’s two dominant ground handlers. Combined revenue at Skyway Aviation Handling Company (SAHCO) and Nigerian Aviation Handling Company (NAHCO) rose from roughly N53.4 billion to N58.4 billion between 2025 and 2026, yet combined cost of sales jumped by almost 40 per cent over the same period, far outpacing revenue growth. ... SAHCO’s net profit margin fell from about 38.6 per cent to 16.7 per cent despite higher turnover, a pattern analysts attribute partly to rising operational levies rather than falling demand. That is why SAHCO’s Managing Director, Adenike Aboderin, has publicly renewed calls for tax relief. “Overheads are rising, inflation is high, forex is unpredictable,” she said, arguing that “tax waivers and government support will go a long way to help ground handlers remain competitive.” ... Freight forwarders echo the concern from the trade side. Seyi Adewale, Managing Director of Mainstream Cargo, estimates Nigeria may be forfeiting between 30 and 40 per cent of potential government revenue to inefficiencies across the cargo value chain, a figure he says outweighs the damage caused by having multiple regulatory agencies at the ports. He also notes that air freight now accounts for more than 80 per cent of total logistics costs in many Nigerian export transactions, meaning naira depreciation against dollar-denominated freight rates compounds every other charge in the stack. ... Layered on top of taxation is a second, less visible cost: offshore insurance placement. Because Nigeria’s underwriting capacity for aviation and cargo risk remains thin, a large share of premiums bypasses the domestic market entirely. Industry estimates cited ahead of the country’s insurance recapitalisation deadline suggest roughly 70 per cent of high-value premiums from specialised assets – including aviation – continue to flow to brokers and reinsurers in London and other global centres, rather than staying within the Nigerian financial system. Incoming Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA) chairman Ebelechukwu Nwachukwu has made domestic underwriting expansion a priority of her administration, as the industry grapples with what analysts describe as significant “underwriting capacity leakage” – an estimated 70 per cent of high-value premiums in aviation and other specialised risk categories still flow to reinsurers in London and other offshore centres. ... The scale of what is at stake is considerable: aviation insurance premiums in Nigeria are projected to approach $2 billion annually, yet airlines argue they are effectively forced into double coverage because aircraft lessors will not recognise domestic policies, pushing carriers back offshore even where local content rules require otherwise. Regulators, however, counter that local capacity is improving. The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) officials say around 40 per cent of Nigerian insurance companies are now competitive enough to underwrite aviation-sector risk and the newly enacted Nigeria Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 is intended to accelerate domestication of aviation and cargo cover. ... None of this is new; clearing agents have clashed with handlers before. When SAHCO and NAHCO doubled cargo processing charges during the festive period, members of the Association of Nigerian Licensed Customs Agents at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos publicly resisted the increase as insensitive to exporters already battling thin margins. The pattern has simply repeated at higher absolute values as fees, FX rates and freight costs have all climbed together. ... For a single shipment, the arithmetic is unforgiving: export levies and registration fees at the warehouse gate, handling and demurrage charges at the terminal, FAAN and NCAA charges on the tarmac, dollar-denominated freight surcharges in transit, and an insurance premium that may never touch a Nigerian balance sheet. Industry voices are broadly aligned on the diagnosis – multiple taxes, overlapping charges and thin local underwriting capacity are compressing margins across the chain – even as they differ on the fix, from tax waivers to insurance domestication to simple regulatory streamlining. Whether the reforms already legislated, including NIIRA 2025, meaningfully unwind that cost stack is likely to be the defining test of Nigerian cargo competitiveness over the next two years.

headline: Dangote Group Looks to Its Own Ships to Overcome Regional Transport Bottlenecks - Ecofin Agency
summary_text: - Dangote Group is considering acquiring its own vessels as it struggles to secure enough shipping capacity for growing exports from Nigeria to West and Central African markets. - The move would deepen Dangote’s control over its logistics chain as cement exports rise and planned refinery expansion is expected to generate even larger regional transport needs. - The plan also reflects a broader regional problem, with limited intra-African shipping capacity, costly road transport and weak rail links keeping logistics costs high across West and Central Africa. ... Dangote Group is considering acquiring its own vessels to transport products from Nigeria to markets in West and Central Africa, according to local media reports citing Sada Ladan-Baki, head of international trade and exports at Dangote Cement. The move comes as the group faces growing difficulty securing enough shipping capacity for its regional exports. ... The challenge is compounded by the high cost of road transport across the region. West and Central Africa lack a sufficiently connected regional rail network to provide a viable alternative to trucking. As a result, regional trade remains heavily dependent on roads, with multiple border crossings, inspections, taxes and other charges adding to costs and delays. For Dangote, those logistics pressures could intensify as production rises. In the oil sector, the group plans to expand the Lekki refinery, including by adding a second distillation unit with capacity of 750,000 barrels per day. Higher volumes bound for regional markets could strengthen the case for securing its own shipping capacity. ... Dangote’s Nigerian operations exported 549,600 tons of cement and clinker in the first quarter of 2026, up 71.6% from a year earlier. Expanding its maritime operations would fit into a broader effort to gain greater control over logistics from production through distribution. Dangote had already signaled in 2024 that it wanted to rely more heavily on maritime transport across its supply and distribution network. The group also announced plans in 2025 to build a deepwater port in Nigeria, intended in part to support its industrial and logistics operations. ... The plan also underscores a longstanding weakness in Africa’s shipping market. Relatively few operators serve regional routes, while available shipping capacity remains insufficient to accommodate growing trade volumes. That leaves African businesses more dependent on major international shipping lines and helps keep logistics costs high. For now, however, the proposal remains preliminary. Dangote has not disclosed how many vessels it could acquire, what types it is considering, how much it might invest or when the ships could enter service.
