headline: Whey Q4 talks stall in extended pricing standoff
summary_text: Whey Q4 talks stall in extended pricing standoff ... # Q4 whey negotiations stall in a pricing standoff ... Whey protein markets are stuck in a Q4 standoff between buyers and sellers, while milk protein concentrate is sold out and climbing on reformulation demand. ... Whey markets are entering a standoff. After a turbulent first half of the year, whey protein concentrate 80 has hit a turning point: high prices pulled in more supply and cooled demand, and that shift is now running straight into the Q4 negotiation window. ... The result isn’t a crash, it’s a stalemate. Western European sellers aren’t desperate, so they’re not chasing the market lower. In the US and Eastern Europe it’s a different picture: sellers there are under more pressure and lower-priced trades are already going through. Buyers, meanwhile, are in no rush either: many are still working through stock built up in the third quarter, and are delaying Q4 coverage rather than accepting today’s asking levels. Whey protein isolate is following a similar pattern, with more US supply reaching Europe but buyers still slow to commit. ... The standoff looks unlikely to hold. Trading volumes are thin, not because the market is genuinely firm, but because neither side wants to move first. Once producers start conceding on price to get Q4 books moving, the correction that follows is likely to be more meaningful than the current calm suggests; it’s a question of timing rather than direction. ... Elsewhere in the whey complex, the picture is the opposite. Sweet whey powder, whey permeate and lactose are all seeing renewed demand as buyers hunt for cheaper alternatives to WPC, alongside firmer SMP pulling lower-protein whey products along with it. None of it is a like-for-like substitute, but there are enough options to matter. ... The standout market is milk protein concentrate 85, which is essentially sold out for the rest of the year across Europe, the US and New Zealand. Reformulation away from WPC toward MPC and other dairy proteins has structurally lifted demand, and the market increasingly resembles where WPC80 stood roughly six months ago: a small production base facing demand it was never built for. Where MPC85 ultimately lands relative to WPC80, and whether the gap between the two keeps narrowing, is the open question heading into the final months of the year.

The problem isn’t that the world is running out of protein. The problem is that the industry’s fastest-growing categories have become heavily dependent on a small number of protein sources. ... Many manufacturers continue to rely on a relatively small group of protein ingredients such as whey, which combines excellent amino acid profiles with digestibility and exceptional functionality across countless applications. But here’s the rub. When an entire industry depends on one ingredient to meet so many different formulation needs, it soon comes under pressure. ... What’s happening in the whey market today is therefore about far more than rising commodity prices. It reflects a combination of long-term trends that are reinforcing one another, creating sustained demand rather than the peaks and corrections experienced in the past. ... Manufacturers have responded accordingly. Protein enrichment is no longer confined to powders and bars, but an ever-evolving product line up aimed at families, older consumers and busy professionals as much as fitness enthusiasts. The European protein ingredients market reflects that momentum, with forecasts valuing it at around US$6.4 billion and continuing to grow at approximately 5% annually. The commercial opportunity is obvious. What is less obvious is the strain on ingredient supply. ... European food-grade whey powder prices have risen by more than 50% since the beginning of 2026, while Whey Protein Concentrate 80 has exceeded €26,000 per tonne in some markets. Availability continues to tighten, lead times have extended, and some suppliers have already allocated production well into 2026 and beyond. ... Larger manufacturers are securing long-term supply agreements wherever possible, while smaller brands are often left managing significant cost increases or reformulating products at relatively short notice. ... Today’s formulators have access to a much broader protein toolbox than they did even a decade ago. Soy continues to offer one of the strongest combinations of functionality, amino acid quality and reliable global supply, while ingredients such as pea, fava bean, chickpea and lentil proteins have all advanced significantly as processing technologies improve flavour, texture and consistency. In addition, processing innovations including precision fermentation and hydrolysed proteins enable manufacturers to overcome long-standing challenges around solubility, mouthfeel and sensory performance. ... Solutions such as IFF’s SUPRO soy protein portfolio demonstrate how carefully selected protein systems can partially or fully replace whey across many applications without compromising quality. The objective should not be to identify one perfect substitute, but to develop formulations that draw on a broader range of protein sources according to the technical, nutritional and commercial requirements of each product. ... ## A new dynamic for protein suppliers This is also changing the role of ingredient suppliers. Conversations increasingly extend beyond sourcing raw materials to understanding functionality, optimising formulations and balancing nutrition, sensory performance, digestibility and supply resilience. Those considerations are becoming inseparable. ... Demand for protein is unlikely to slow. If anything, it will continue to grow as populations age, GLP-1 medicines become more widely adopted, and consumers expect more from the foods they buy every day. Protein’s success has transformed the food industry. Yet that success is also exposing the risks of relying too heavily on too few protein sources. The next generation of innovation will not be driven by adding more protein, but by creating more resilient ways to deliver it.

headline: Lactalis buys Saputo UK for $1.34B, whey prices up 76%, Canada tariffs loom
summary_text: , Consolidation, a genuine demand shock, and a live trade deadline are all colliding in dairy this week — Lactalis just landed its fourth acquisition in two months, GLP-1 drugs are reshaping whey pricing, and Canada has less than 48 hours before 50% US tariffs hit its dairy exports. Here's today's top stories Dairy Chain edition, follow ... Lactalis has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Saputo's UK dairy division for approximately £988 million ($1.34 billion), the companies announced August 14. The deal hands Lactalis five UK manufacturing facilities and a portfolio of major British brands, including Cathedral City and Davidstow cheddar, Wensleydale Creamery cheese, Country Life butter, and the Clover and Utterly Butterly margarine lines. Saputo UK generated roughly £800 million ($1.2 billion) in revenue over the past four quarters, about 7% of Saputo's consolidated sales, with 94% of that revenue earned domestically in Britain across a 1,300-person workforce. ... Lactalis says the acquisition will make it the market leader in the UK cheddar, butter, and margarine categories. The deal is expected to close by the end of Q1 calendar 2027, pending regulatory approval, with both companies confirming operations will continue as normal through the transition. Saputo said proceeds will go toward reducing debt leverage and funding organic growth and future acquisitions elsewhere in its portfolio. ... This is Lactalis's fourth acquisition in just two months, following deals for UK protein brand Protein Works, French dairy group Triballat, and select cheese assets (including the Oka and Saint-Hyacinthe brands and facilities) from Canadian cooperative Agropur. It also follows Lactalis's win last year of Fonterra's global consumer dairy business for roughly NZ$3.8 billion — meaning the privately held French group has now built a genuinely global acquisition pace across two continents in under 12 months. ... US whey powder prices rose 76% year-over-year in June, with spot prices up 60% since the start of 2026, according to a Rabobank agribusiness report. The driver is a structural shift in demand: GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy are widely prescribed alongside guidance to maintain protein intake, since rapid weight loss on these drugs carries real risk of lean muscle mass depletion. That's converting whey and casein from a bodybuilder/sports-nutrition niche into what Rabobank's senior animal proteins analyst Jen Corkran called a genuinely mainstream demand story, compounding with existing high-protein trends among Millennial and Gen Z consumers and clinical nutrition needs among aging populations. ... New Zealand processors are moving to capture the margin. Westland Milk Products, owned by China's Yili Group, is actively expanding its lactoferrin processing facility in Hokitika to meet demand, and Yili Oceania's chief executive identified the US specifically as the epicenter of the structural shift. Separately, US industry data shows the market is now described as the tightest in years, with premium whey isolate reaching roughly $14 per pound and European 80% whey protein concentrate hitting a record average of €26,450 ($30,518) per metric ton in late May — more than double where it stood less than a year earlier. Analysts attribute the supply side of the squeeze to constrained cheesemaking and whey-processing capacity rather than any shortfall in raw milk itself; every pound of cheese produced yields roughly nine pounds of whey as a byproduct, so more processing capacity, not more milk, is the actual bottleneck. ... Why it matters for buyers: this is a structural, not cyclical, demand shift, meaning current pricing likely doesn't ease until new whey-processing capacity actually comes online, a multi-year proposition. Buyers of whey-based ingredients for protein-fortified products should expect continued tight supply and elevated pricing, and should treat whey and casein pricing separately from the broader dairy commodity complex — as several dairy analysts note, headline dairy indices can be soft even while whey runs at record highs, since each dairy product category has its own distinct supply-demand balance. ... President Trump signed three Section 338 proclamations on July 20 imposing an additional 50% tariff on specific Canadian dairy, alcohol, and motor vehicle goods, set to take effect at 12:01am Eastern on August 19 — with no exemption for goods otherwise compliant under USMCA. The dairy list alone covers approximately 52 tariff classifications, including specified milk and cream products, whey, lactose, and casein; cheese, butter, yogurt, fluid milk, cream, sour cream, and ice cream are exempted from this particular measure. The stated justification is Canada's supply management system and its tariff-rate quota administration, which the US dairy industry has long argued restricts full use of the market access Canada committed to under USMCA. ... With the deadline now inside 48 hours, Canadian and US trade negotiators have been meeting daily in Washington, with talks continuing right through the weekend — Canada's trade minister Dominic LeBlanc held a virtual meeting with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Sunday, August 16, described by a LeBlanc spokesperson as "constructive," with both sides "taking stock" of progress made by their negotiating teams. The White House estimates the combined tariffs cover roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. On the dairy specifics, Canada's chief trade negotiator has indicated some flexibility around how existing CUSMA tariff-rate quotas are administered — which currently grant US dairy producers access to roughly 3.5% to 3.9% of the Canadian market — while maintaining that Canada's core supply management system itself will not be dismantled. Canadian officials have also signaled that if no deal is reached, Canada is preparing "surgically targeted" retaliatory measures — not counter-tariffs, but tools aimed at restricting US access to Canadian procurement contracts, critical minerals, and energy. ... Canadian dairy farmer groups continue warning the government against making concessions on supply management regardless of the economic pressure. On the US side, the National Milk Producers Federation and US Dairy Export Council continue pointing to Canada's dairy import growth — from $251.7 million in 2021 to $432.7 million in 2025 — as evidence Canada has room to open its market further rather than restrict it. ... Why it matters for buyers: with roughly two days left before the deadline, this is genuinely live and could move in either direction — a last-minute framework deal, a partial rollback, or the tariffs taking full effect as scheduled. Buyers with Canadian-sourced whey, lactose, casein, or milk powder in their supply chain should confirm with suppliers whether shipments can be accelerated ahead of the August 19 effective date, and should have contingency sourcing identified in case the 50% duty sticks — note that finished cheese, butter, and fluid milk are exempted from this specific tariff, so the exposure is concentrated in dairy ingredients rather than consumer-facing dairy products. ... Today's three stories point in different directions but share a common thread: dairy's supply chain is being reshaped simultaneously by consolidation, a genuine external demand shock, and geopolitics — and all three are moving fast enough that positions taken this week could look very different by next week. Watch the August 19 tariff deadline most closely; it lands before your next edition, and however it resolves will have immediate, concrete effects on Canadian dairy ingredient sourcing costs. Also worth tracking: whether the Synlait takeover speculation resolves into a formal proposal despite this week's denial, and whether whey pricing shows any signs of the capacity expansions (like Westland's Hokitika project) starting to bite.

headline: WPC80 climb stalls ahead of Q4 whey contracting
summary_text: WPC80 climb stalls ahead of Q4 whey contracting ... # Whey protein's climb stalls before Q4 contracting ... Whether that makes the market bearish is a separate question, and Vesper is not convinced it has arrived yet. Global demand for WPC80 is still substantial, and Q4 has historically been a heavier purchasing quarter as buyers cover Black Friday and the run into the holidays. Manufacturers have raised output and sold a good share of it forward, and still expect to be sold out before demand runs out. The turning point looks closer than it did, but Vesper puts it more than a couple of weeks away. Whey protein isolate has become a made-to-order market, available in any volume at the right premium. That premium over WPC80 has narrowed, partly because reformulation moved away from isolate too. ... Vesper’s Q4 view has whey pricing holding around current levels, and does not see enough in the shift to push WPC80 below the €25,000/t mark before the quarter starts. headline: How membrane filtration can transform milk into high-value ingredients | Dairy Foods
summary_text: Consumer preferences are becoming more varied, with demand growing for higher-protein, lactose-free and plant-based products alongside traditional dairy categories. According to NielsenIQ, U.S. data showed sales of lactose-free and lactose-reduced dairy milk grew by around 14% over the past year, while plant-based milk continues to represent a significant part of the global dairy alternatives market. ... For dairy producers, this creates pressure to expand product portfolios and respond quickly to changing demand, without also significantly increasing operational complexity or cost. At the same time, demand for specialized dairy ingredients is rising, particularly in areas such as sports nutrition and functional foods. According to data from Dutch firm DCA Market Intelligence, across Europe alone, food-grade whey powder prices have gone up by more than 50% highlighting a broader shift in the dairy market, where protein components are gaining value. ... This shift is one reason membrane filtration is receiving renewed attention across the industry. Once viewed mainly as a processing efficiency tool, membrane technologies are now helping producers recover more value from existing streams, develop new ingredients to meet rising consumer demand and extend product portfolios into adjacent categories. ... Membrane filtration has long been used in dairy processing to separate, concentrate and standardize milk and whey streams. Depending on the application, technologies such as reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, ultrafiltration and microfiltration can separate water, fat and proteins for further use in other parts of production. ... this has delivered operational benefits around consistency, yield and processing efficiency ... increasingly, dairy ... on throughput, ... those systems can help create higher-value outputs. ... Whey is a clear example. Previously treated primarily as a by-product of cheese production, it is now a valuable source of ingredients used in sports nutrition and functional food categories. By concentrating whey proteins, dairy producers can participate in higher-margin ingredient markets while reducing transport and handling volumes at the same time. An example of this is cheese producer Mammen Dairies in Denmark, which worked with Tetra Pak on a reverse osmosis membrane filtration solution designed for whey concentration. The system removes around 75% of the water from the whey stream before further processing. The concentrated whey protein is then sold for use in sports nutrition ingredients. ... The same concept applies more broadly across dairy ingredients. Membrane filtration can be used to fractionate proteins into specific components with different functional applications. In white milk processing, for example, microfiltration can separate casein and whey proteins. The whey proteins can be concentrated using ultrafiltration, after which calcium phosphate can be extracted from the lactose in the permeate and used to fortify products, including plant-based beverages. ... it requires entirely ... set ups. New categories may be growing, but large capital investments are risky, especially when demand isn’t stable. In this case, processing flexibility can lower that barrier. Arna, a dairy producer in Iceland, started exploring plant-based products after noticing growing consumer interest in oat-based alternatives. The company already used ultrafiltration technology for lactose-free skyr and yoghurt production, which meant it could adapt existing capabilities rather than going right back to the start. Working with filtration specialists, Arna tested different membrane setups for oat processing and eventually developed a range of oat-based skyr products in multiple flavors. ... As dairy markets continue to fragment, growth is no longer concentrated in a small number of standardized products. Producers now need to supply a wider mix of formats, nutritional profiles and ingredient combinations, often in shorter production runs. Flexible processing can help them do that by using existing knowledge and infrastructure to move into new categories with less disruption. ... At the same time, there is pressure to improve resource efficiency across manufacturing operations. Recovering more usable material from existing streams, reducing waste and increasing output value from the same raw inputs are all becoming more important operational priorities. ... While membrane filtration may not be the answer to every challenge facing dairy producers, consumer preferences will inevitably continue to shift, and product trends will keep changing across regions and categories. So, what membrane systems do offer is adaptability. For many processors, the priority is building operations that can respond to both traditional dairy and newer product categories. That may involve producing higher-protein dairy products, supplying functional ingredients, recovering more value from whey streams or extending into plant-based applications where it makes commercial sense. The dairy producers likely to be in the strongest position over the next decade will be those that can adjust without repeatedly rebuilding their operations around each new trend. That will mean investing in processing systems that allow for more flexibility in how raw materials, side streams and ingredients are used over time. In a market that is becoming more specialized and less predictable, the ability to adapt existing infrastructure may prove just as important as launching the next new product category.

headline: Protein brands grapple with soaring whey costs amid heightened demand
summary_text: Whey protein has hit headlines again in recent weeks following a surge in wholesale pricing, with some suppliers reportedly already sold out for the rest of 2026. (StefaNikolic / Getty Images) ... ## Whey protein prices have increased five-fold since 2023 according to new data, with demand continuing to grow faster than available production capacity. ... Its recent surge in popularity has pushed prices to record levels, with data from commodity intelligence platform Vesper Tool revealing that WPC80 (whey protein concentrate containing at least 80% protein by weight) now costs $32,000 per metric tonne ($14.50/lb), up from $5,500 per tonne ($2.49/lb) during the same period in 2023. ... “The market is responding, as these high prices are pushing dairy cooperatives to invest in new production capacity and forcing buyers to blend different protein types. While this will eventually help push prices back down, it is not currently enough to cool ... Because whey protein is a natural by-product of the cheese-making process, its supply is closely linked to cheese manufacturing volumes. But while the cheese market is growing at a CAGR of around 4% to 5%, demand for whey is growing at a much faster rate. ... In addition, ... manufacturing requires specialized equipment such as membrane filtration and spray-drying infrastructure. Although plans to ramp up production are underway, building new lines and expanding production facilities ... This is creating a disparity between demand and supply, with a notable surge in price occurring over the past 12-to-18 months, according to Mike O’Leary, head of product at Elite Sports Nutrition (ESN). ... ## Cost pressures felt particularly strongly in Europe ... The resulting price increase, however, has been felt particularly strongly in the European market, where prices fluctuate more frequently, O’Leary noted. ... “Across the industry, rising raw material costs have become one of the defining challenges of the current market environment,” he said. “In Europe, whey protein prices are typically negotiated on a quarterly basis rather than through annual contracts. As a result, changes in supply and demand dynamics tend to be reflected relatively quickly in market pricing.” ... A number of whey-focused brands have reported slow growth as a result. For example, in 2024, THG—which owns MyProtein— reported a loss of £147.9 million ($195.8 million), driven by factors including high material costs, inflation, high investment and acquisitions. ... Matthew Moulding, CEO of THG, said the company was grappling with an “unprecedented commodity cost environment”, leading the company’s nutrition arm to further diversify its product offering beyond whey protein, to vitamins and minerals, snacks, chilled and frozen food, and active wear. ... During a conference call following the company’s annual financial results, Damian Sanders, THG’s chief financial officer, told analysts and investors that the company was also experimenting with protein innovation. ... “We are proactively managing our product mix,” he said. “We have successfully driven category diversification with strong growth across non-whey categories such as creatine, active wear and hydration. Protein innovation is also well underway as we leverage a wider range of sources to deliver high-quality, trend-led products while building a more resilient product portfolio to navigate market fluctuations.” ... ESN has implemented similar measures, reviewing sourcing strategies, operational efficiencies and portfolio planning, while protecting product quality to ensure consumer confidence. ... While the whey protein market is notorious for its volatility, Nick Morgan, managing director of Nutrition Integrated, predicts that heightened demand is likely to continue, suggesting that high prices probably are, too. ... “The increase in demand is not going anywhere—we’re not going to suddenly demonize protein,” he said. “There is an assumption that prices may drop a little bit, but they will not go anywhere close to where they’ve been previously. So, to some extent, the industry needs to reset itself so there is a new benchmark, or a new north, for the prices they can expect for WPC [whey protein concentrate] and WPI [whey protein isolate].” ... “Sadly, I think there will be a lot of change and fall out,” he said. “Firstly, many small-to-medium sized brands will struggle to survive, particularly those where whey protein is the majority driver of their business. Beyond that, almost all brands are looking to pull on several levers to better improve their margin mix and evolve their business model to mitigate the risk of whey protein volatility.” ... Morgan said brands have several options. They may choose to focus on diversifying their product offering, lessening the impact ... high whey protein prices by selling more of other products. Creatine, is one example of a product which is currently performing well. ... Brands could also increase the price of their whey protein products, or play with ‘pack type architecture’, i.e. changing pack sizes and serving sizes. New product development and reformulation present another opportunity i.e. experimenting with other protein sources, such as plant and casein. ... ESN, for example, has opted not to change product specifications or replace premium protein sources with lower-quality alternatives, as according to O’Leary, the company believes protecting product quality and consumer confidence is more important than pursuing short-term solutions. ... “The current environment is demonstrating the importance of resilient supply chains, strong brands and long-term partnerships,” he said. “Companies that have built consumer trust and operational capabilities over many years are generally better positioned to navigate periods of market volatility.”

headline: Dairy giants move into activ nutrition as protein demand surges

Soon, protein became central to industry growth, and dairy companies increasingly began behaving like nutrition businesses rather than traditional food producers. On June 1, dairy giant Lactalis announced that it had acquired Britain’s active nutrition brand Protein Works—entering to compete for its share of the rapidly expanding consumer-facing active nutrition market. ... It began investing in whey protein production capabilities and launched the Arla Protein brand in 2015, entering the consumer protein shake and snack market. ... - FrieslandCampina shifted from commodity dairy into specialized protein ingredients between 2010 and 2015, expanding its whey and casein protein capabilities and developing advanced nutrition systems for sports and medical applications. ... - Irish dairy cooperative Glanbia also began shifting towards a modern nutrition business status in the early 2000s. Between 2017 and 2019, it expanded through acquisitions such as Atrium Innovations, adding supplement brands like Garden of Life, and in 2020, it acquired Vital Proteins, strengthening its position in collagen and lifestyle protein. More recently, it has expanded across medical, sports recovery, and ready-to-drink nutrition, including the recently announced acquisition of Yfood. ... - While it did not start as a dairy cooperative, Danone began moving toward health-focused dairy in the early 2000s, linking dairy with gut health, protein, and wellness. In 2017, it restructured its portfolio around health nutrition and scaled its Nutricia medical nutrition business. From 2023 onwards, it pushed high-protein dairy into mainstream wellness and connected clinical nutrition with sports performance. It further accelerated this strategy with the recent acquisition of the high-protein meal replacement brand Huel, strengthening its position in complete, functional nutrition alongside brands like Activia, Alpro and Aptamil. ... This advantage becomes increasingly important as global demand for protein continues to rise. Meanwhile, whey protein supply remains constrained, with demand continuing to outpace available raw materials, converting access to high-quality protein into a strategic asset rather than simply an input cost. ... FrieslandCampina recently announced a €90 million investment to expand whey protein production, citing strong demand and ongoing supply constraints in the market and emphasizing its end-to-end control of the supply chain as a key differentiator. Even when a protein source might not be the most optimal for a specific formulation, suppliers are seeing the necessity to invest in it because consumer demand drives decisions, Guus Aerts, global director of marketing and product strategy at FrieslandCampina Ingredients said following the investment announcement. This creates a demand-led cycle where ingredient companies and dairy suppliers scale up the proteins consumers already buy, expanding production around established ingredients like whey because they deliver consistent demand and sales. ... According to data from commodity intelligence platform Vesper Tool, WPC80 (whey protein concentrate containing at least 80% protein) has surged sharply in value, rising to about $32,000 per metric tonne, up from roughly $5,500 per tonne in 2023. Vesper’s EU Price Index also places WPC80 at around €16,900 per tonne in the EU and €18,204 per tonne in the US. ... At the same time, data from the market data and analysis company focused on the dairy and agricultural commodity sector, DCA Market Intelligence, shows that food-grade whey powder has climbed to a record level of around €1,700 per tonne, up from approximately €1,100–€1,200 per tonne at the start of the year, reflecting broad-based strength in whey markets driven by rising protein demand and tightening supply conditions. ... “This gives dairy companies the opportunity to create more value from the same liter of milk,” Baan said. “We are already seeing this in the market. According to DCA Market Intelligence data, food-grade whey powder prices have risen by more than 50% this year to record levels, showing how valuable protein has become.” ... Whey supply is inherently tied to cheese production, meaning it cannot be expanded independently or rapidly increased in response to rising demand. In the short term, supply is therefore relatively fixed. At the same time, demand for protein-rich products continues to grow. ... And for now at least, the market shows no signs of slowing, with key market signals indicating that the dairy-to-active-nutrition transition is continuing to accelerate. ... “One of the clearest signals is whey pricing,” Baan said. “When whey prices perform much better than traditional dairy commodities, it shows that protein demand is becoming a major driver of value in the dairy sector.” ... Another, he noted, is the continued investment, adding that dairy companies increased investing in protein processing capacity and protein-focused product suggests they expect further growth. ... “Retail sales of protein drinks, protein yogurts and sports nutrition products are also important indicators,” he added. “A peak would likely be visible through weaker demand growth, rising inventories, falling price premiums and new production capacity growing faster than demand. headline: New commodities report shows Pacific Agricultural exports to Australia more than triple in five years - Post Courier
summary_text: Australia’s appetite for Pacific agricultural products is growing rapidly, and so too is the region’s interest in supplying them. ... A new Pacific Trade Invest Australia report, Australia’s Imports from the Pacific 2026 Review, shows imports of selected agricultural commodities from Pacific Island countries have increased more than threefold over the past five years. ... At the same time, more than 200 exporters, government officials, biosecurity agencies and agribusiness professionals from across the Pacific recently joined a webinar hosted by Pacific Trade Invest Australia in partnership with the Australian Department of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries (DAFF), underlining the strong interest in expanding agricultural exports to Australia. ... The latest report draws on Australian Bureau of Statistics trade data compiled by DAFF. It found the value of selected agricultural imports from Pacific Island countries rose 3.1 times between 2020 and 2025, representing a compound annual growth rate of about 25 percent. ... The report examines Australia’s imports of key Pacific commodities including green coffee, cocoa beans, coconut oil, cassava, vanilla, taro, ginger and seafood, providing exporters, governments and investors with a clearer picture of where commercial opportunities are emerging. ... “Trade between the Pacific and Australia continues to evolve, creating new opportunities for Pacific exporters, Australian importers and the broader regional economy,” Martin said. ... The report also complements PTI Australia’s wider work to prepare exporters for the Australian market. During the recent webinar, DAFF specialists outlined Australia’s biosecurity framework, international phytosanitary standards and the practical steps exporters need to take to meet market access requirements. The message was clear – while opportunities exist, exporters that understand Australia’s biosecurity and market access requirements are far better positioned to convert demand into sales. ... Green coffee was the strongest contributor to growth. Papua New Guinea, the Pacific’s only supplier of green coffee beans to Australia, exported more than AUD$112.5 million (US$80.43 million) in 2025, making coffee the region’s largest agricultural export to Australia by value. While rising global coffee prices contributed significantly, the Pacific’s share of Australia’s green coffee imports increased from 6.5 percent in 2020 to 9.3 percent in 2025. ... Coconut oil and cocoa also recorded strong gains. The Pacific’s share of Australia’s coconut oil imports rose from 3.7 percent to 13.4 percent between 2020 and 2025, while its share of cocoa bean imports increased from 15.3 percent to 25.3 percent. Fiji remained the largest coconut oil supplier, with Vanuatu emerging as a strong performer, while Papua New Guinea continued to lead cocoa exports, supported by growing exports from Vanuatu and Solomon Islands. ... The report also highlights Australia’s reliance on the Pacific for staple food products. In 2025, the region supplied 79 percent of Australia’s imported taro and more than 55 percent of imported cassava by value. Tonga and Fiji remained the leading cassava exporters, while Solomon Islands recorded the fastest growth. ... Vanilla exports also recovered, with the Pacific accounting for 38.7 percent of Australia’s vanilla imports in 2025 and Papua New Guinea increasing export volumes by 66 percent over the past three years. ... Not every commodity moved in the same direction, however. Ginger recorded the sharpest decline of all products reviewed. The Pacific’s share of Australia’s ginger imports fell from 15.8 percent in 2024 to just 1.3 percent in 2025, with Fiji, the only Pacific supplier during the year, experiencing a sharp drop in export volumes. Whole coconut exports also continued their long-term decline, leaving Samoa and Tonga as the region’s only active suppliers by 2025. ... For PTI Australia, the report and the recent webinar tell different parts of the same story. One highlights where Australian demand is growing, while the other reflects the drive of Pacific exporters to understand what’s needed to compete successfully in Australia. As Australian consumers continue to embrace Pacific products, the challenge is becoming less about identifying opportunities than helping more businesses seize them…. PACNEWS

headline: Fiji targets 3 million tonnes of sugar cane to support viable sustainable aviation fuel, but faces investment and policy hurdles - FijiGlobalNews
summary_text: Fiji would need to harvest about three million tonnes of sugar cane annually to produce enough feedstock for commercially viable sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), Civil Aviation Minister Viliame Gavoka has warned — a target that industry leaders say is achievable but will require major investment and systemic fixes. ... Speaking about the 2026–2031 Civil Aviation Master Plan, Gavoka described SAF as “challenging” but said Fiji could produce it from sugarcane if the country could scale up cane production to roughly three million tonnes a year, a volume he said would make SAF production economic and position Fiji as a regional producer. “Those are some of the challenges that we have,” he added, underlining that supply constraints are a central obstacle to any local SAF ambition. ... Lautoka Cane Producers Association president Bala Dass welcomed the ambition but stressed it would need concerted support. “Producing a consistent three million tonnes each year is ambitious but possible with the right resources,” Dass said, listing priorities that must be addressed: new high‑yielding cane varieties and more efficient mill infrastructure at Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), secured land tenure for growers and a reliable harvesting workforce. “Give the farmers what they need for that to happen,” he said, noting Fiji once produced between three and four million tonnes in its stronger years. ... The call to scale comes against a backdrop of decline. Government figures show annual cane crushed fell from 1.73 million tonnes in 2020 to 1.33 million tonnes in 2024, leaving the sector well short of the level Gavoka says is needed for SAF. The drop has been fuelled by a mix of challenges that have surfaced across the industry this year: pre‑season burnt cane losses for growers, a fire at the Rarawai Sugar Mill that forced cane to be redirected to Lautoka and prompted temporary compensation measures, and concerns about land salinity and stalled planting on some state leases. ... Recent government interventions provide context for the SAF debate. The Ministry of Sugar and the Sugar Cane Growers Council have rolled out relief and rehabilitation packages for farmers affected by fires and mill disruptions, including cash support for dozens of growers ahead of the 2025 season and a $15‑per‑tonne compensation scheme for cane redirected from Rarawai to Lautoka. Sugar Industry Minister Charan Jeath Singh has repeatedly emphasised the government’s commitment to sustaining grower participation while the sector addresses longer‑term structural issues. ... Industry leaders say the shift toward SAF would not simply be an agricultural challenge but also require industrial and policy changes. Dass and others point to the need for upgraded milling capacity and efficiency at FSC to process much larger volumes, investment in agronomy and planting of high‑yielding varieties, resolved land tenure to encourage replanting and expansion, and measures to reduce pre‑harvest burning that can wipe out crops and deter investment. ... If the government proceeds with SAF ambitions tied to the Civil Aviation Master Plan, stakeholders say detailed feasibility work, financing plans and clear timelines will be essential. For now, Gavoka’s declaration has reframed the sugar sector’s recovery not only as an economic and social issue for rural communities but as a potential feedstock strategy tied to Fiji’s aviation and climate ambitions — one that will require reversing the recent decline in cane production and significant capital and policy support.

summary_text: Agriculture Minister Tomasi Tunabuna has warned that modernising Fiji’s beleaguered sugar industry must go hand-in-hand with practical support for communities being pushed out of cane, saying the government must prepare alternatives for growers who can no longer make a living from sugarcane alone. ... Speaking on the Fiji Sugar Corporation’s 2023 and 2024 annual reports, Tunabuna pointed to rising production costs, labour shortages, contested land tenure, and climate impacts as mounting pressures that are forcing some growers to abandon cane. “I have consistently maintained that if Fiji is serious about helping the modern and competitive sugar industry, then we must be prepared to make necessary changes. We cannot continue doing things the same way and expect a different result,” he said, backing recent recommendations for reform and modernisation. ... Tunabuna stressed the point that supporting farmers does not mean keeping everyone in cane production indefinitely. “We cannot simply tell our farmers to leave the industry without providing practical alternatives. This means identifying opportunities for farmers to diversify into other crops and agricultural activities that are sustainable to their land, location, and market opportunities,” he said. He urged policy-makers to balance efficiency gains in milling and production with measures to protect livelihoods and community resilience. ... His intervention comes amid a string of recent disruptions and relief measures that have exposed structural weaknesses across the sector. In September, a fire at the Rarawai Sugar Mill in Ba forced cane to be redirected to Lautoka and prompted temporary relief packages for affected growers. Earlier in the season the government extended pre-crush assistance to farmers hit by burnt cane in regions including Rakiraki, while other communities have sought help after land was declared too saline for viable cane cultivation. ... Tunabuna told reporters he supports the recommendation by the parliamentary Standing Committee on Economic Affairs for broader reform, but warned any changes must recognise “the human dimension” — ensuring farmers and communities are not left without options. That human-centred approach, he said, would require coordinated programmes to help growers transition to alternative land uses without creating new dependencies. ... An EU-backed study is currently examining agricultural diversification options, Tunabuna said, and the ministry intends to use the study’s findings to design long-term, sustainable programmes that enable farmers to shift into other crops or agricultural activities. The minister emphasised that diversification plans must be tailored to individual land capability, proximity to markets, and the skills and aspirations of farming families. ... headline: inDepth I The sugar dilemma - Call for new direction as industry faces challenges - The Fiji Times
summary_text: SINGH THE sugar industry is draining Fiji’s economy, and the country can no longer afford to continue supporting it in its current form, says People’s Alliance party (PA) president Ratu Josefa Dimuri. ... Ratu Josefa believes major changes are needed, including considering private management of the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), closing the mills on Viti Levu and making Labasa the main centre for sugar production. ... His comments come as Government continues to invest millions of dollars into the industry while facing problems with cane supply, ageing mills, labour shortages and rising costs. ... Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna has acknowledged that Government was investing significant money into the sector while returns remained a concern. ... Mr Tunabuna had also confirmed Government was paying about $18million each year to service debts, including money owed to the Exim Bank of India. ... He suggested that the Government consider closing the mills on Viti Levu and concentrating sugar production in Labasa. ... “I would like to suggest that we close the mills in Viti Levu and only concentrate sugar production at Labasa. We should improve the quality of the crop and increase production there.” ... the proposal comes ... Labasa mill ... The mill stopped crushing during the first three weeks of the current crushing season because of low or no cane supply. ... abuna said the start of the crushing season had been difficult because of the fuel crisis and other disruptions. ... Farmers had signed the Master Award Growers Agreement and decided to continue harvesting. ... The Labasa mill needs between 5500 and 6000 tonnes of cane each day to keep operating. ... However, it has been receiving only about 3500 to 4000 tonnes. The shortage means the mill cannot operate at its full capacity. ... Fiji’s aging sugar mills is another major concern. ... Mr Tunabuna said the mills needed regular maintenance because of their age and defended the practice of closing mills on Sundays. ... But Ratu Josefa believes the continued cost of keeping the industry operating is becoming too heavy for the country. ... The future of FSC could also involve private ownership. ... Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has confirmed that selling FSC to a private company is an option. ... However, he said FSC was a strategic asset and Government needed to consider its importance before making any decision. ... “Selling is an option, but there are certain things that we call strategic assets, and these are strategic assets,” he said. “They belong to the Government, and what we can do is improve the performance of the industry.” ... Mr Rabuka said Government was focused on improving the performance of the sugar industry while considering its future. ... A special committee on the sugar industry is consulting farmers and other stakeholders about the problems facing the sector. ... The committee has already visited sugar-growing areas in the West and is expected to visit the North. ... Sugar provides income mainly during the crushing season, while other crops could be harvested and sold throughout the year. ... The problems facing the sugar industry have also led to Fiji importing sugar. ... Mr Tunabuna said the decision was made to ensure there was enough sugar available for consumers. ... “The importation was based on the need that we have for sugar,” he said. ... He said delays in harvesting and low cane supply at the start of the crushing season may have contributed to the need for imports. ... FSC had prepared for possible supply problems by keeping sugar stocks available. ... “FSC also knew that was going to come, so we wanted to make sure that we had some available sugar in stock in case some retailers were going to restrict sales of their sugar.,” ... Farmers and harvesting operators are also dealing with changes in mechanical harvesting rates. ... The Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission reduced the mechanical harvesting rate from $24.63 a tonne to $20.52 a tonne after fuel prices dropped. The new rate is 16.7 per cent lower than the previous interim rate. ... Some harvesting operators have raised concerns that the lower rate could affect their ability to continue providing services. ... The sugar industry now faces several major challenges at the same time. ... Farmers are struggling with cane supply and production costs. Mills are old and require regular maintenance. Government is spending millions of dollars to keep the industry operating, while FSC continues to carry debt. ... At the same time, Fiji is importing sugar to ensure consumers have enough supply. ... Ratu Josefa believes the country must now consider a different approach. ... He wants Government to focus sugar production in Labasa, consider private management of FSC and encourage farmers to move into crops that could provide higher and more regular returns. ... Mr Rabuka said FSC remains a strategic asset and Government is looking at ways to improve its performance. ... The special committee on the sugar industry’s consultations could help determine what happens next. ... For farmers and communities that depend on sugar, the decision will have major consequences. ... The debate is no longer simply about how to produce more sugar. It is about whether Fiji can continue paying the rising cost of keeping the industry alive or whether it is time to change the way the country produces, manages and earns from agriculture.

headline: Indonesia says molasses import halt lifted prices — Shev IO
summary_text: Indonesia says molasses import halt lifted prices — Shev IO ... July 2026, 09:00 UTC # Indonesia says molasses import halt stabilized sugarcane farmer prices ... Indonesia’s agriculture minister says stopping molasses imports lifted and stabilized domestic prices after imported supply had pressured the market. The government now wants to raise sugarcane yields from 60 tonnes to 100 tonnes through technology. ... Indonesia’s decision to halt molasses imports has lifted and stabilized domestic prices, easing pressure on sugarcane farmers, Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman told President Prabowo Subianto. According to Kompas.com, Amran said imported molasses had previously pushed prices down, but the market rose immediately after Prabowo ordered the inflow stopped through a presidential instruction. ... The minister presented the import measure as a direct response to complaints from growers. He said farmers had been suffering when imported molasses entered the country and depressed prices, but were no longer facing the same distress after the ban. Kompas.com did not report the previous or current price, the volume of imports affected, the countries supplying the product or the formal duration of the restriction. ... Molasses is a by-product of sugar processing, so its price affects the value recovered from crushing sugarcane in addition to the revenue generated by sugar itself. A stronger domestic molasses market can improve returns along the processing chain, although the impact on individual farmers depends on purchasing arrangements between growers and mills. For processors and industrial users, the import halt also makes domestic availability and pricing more important. The report did not identify the industries buying the molasses or describe any effect on their input costs. ... Amran said Indonesia must now improve sugarcane productivity. He set out an ambition to raise output from 60 tonnes to 100 tonnes, while citing yields of 120 tonnes and 130 tonnes in India and saying Brazil had achieved similarly high performance. He told Prabowo that reaching higher yields would require advanced technology, without specifying a timetable, investment amount or cultivation program. ... The productivity target matters because restricting imports can support prices but does not by itself increase the volume of cane or molasses available to processors. Raising yields toward 100 tonnes would expand output from existing farmland if the target is achieved, potentially giving mills more raw material while supporting domestic supply. During the visit, Prabowo also inspected heavy equipment and watched farmers harvesting sugarcane. He greeted several growers and held discussions with Amran and Coordinating Minister for Food Affairs Zulkifli Hasan. No additional import, production or price measures were announced in the Kompas.com report. ... > “Stopping imports lifted molasses prices immediately, according to the agriculture minister. That gives sugarcane growers and mills more value from a key processing by-product, but industrial buyers must now rely more heavily on domestic supply. > > The larger constraint is productivity. Indonesia wants to move from 60 tonnes to 100 tonnes, while India already reaches 120 tonnes and 130 tonnes. Price protection can offer short-term relief, but technology and higher field yields will determine whether processors receive enough cane without creating tighter supply for molasses users.”

headline: Westpac warns Fiji sugar faces long-term viability challenges, urges phased transition with reforms and investment - FijiGlobalNews
summary_text: Westpac has raised fresh doubts about the long-term viability of Fiji’s sugar industry, urging policymakers to consider a managed, gradual transition away from cane production unless fundamental reforms and large capital investments are put in place. The warning appears in the bank’s FY2026-27 National Budget Review, released this month, and comes as the sector continues to reel from recent operational shocks and longstanding structural disadvantages. ... The review says the industry has been rendered largely uncompetitive since Fiji lost preferential European Union sugar prices — once nearly three times the world market rate — and now faces direct competition from major producers such as India, Brazil and Australia. “Today, Fiji must compete against large-scale producers… which benefit from lower labour costs, greater economies of scale, larger state subsidies and more advanced technology,” Westpac states, noting those comparative advantages make it difficult for Fiji to match prices and margins. ... Westpac highlights several domestic constraints that hamper competitiveness: small average farm sizes, long transport distances to mills and ports, and persistent dependence on manual harvesting. The bank says mechanisation has not been a panacea. Hilly terrain remains unsuitable for many machines, and cane harvested mechanically carries higher levels of extraneous matter — dirt and trash — that reduces sugar recovery in Fiji’s ageing mills, which were designed to process manually cut cane. According to the review, a successful switch to mechanisation would demand substantial capital expenditure that Fiji currently lacks. ... The bank underscores the social and political complexity of any major shift. It warns against abrupt closures, noting about 10,000 growers still rely directly on sugar production — roughly one percent of the population, or about four percent when family members are included. Rather than immediate divestment, Westpac recommends a “gradual, long-term roadmap” of reforms and assistance to help farmers diversify into alternative livelihoods. ... The assessment arrives amid a series of recent disruptions that have laid bare the industry’s fragility. In September, a fire at the Rarawai Sugar Mill in Ba forced cane to be redirected to Lautoka; the government announced compensation of $15 per tonne for redirected cane and various relief measures. The Ministry of Sugar also extended pre-crush burnt-cane support earlier this year, allocating $101,725 to assist 58 affected farmers. Sugar Industry Minister Charan Jeath Singh, accompanied by Acting Prime Minister Biman Prasad on a visit to the damaged mill, has overseen emergency responses while reiterating the government’s commitment to harvest the season’s cane. ... Westpac’s intervention reframes the debate from short-term crisis management toward long-term strategy. Its analysis adds weight to calls — from economists and some industry observers — for a candid appraisal of whether sustained public or private investment in the traditional sugar value chain is the best use of resources, or whether targeted programs to retrain growers, improve land use, and build alternative rural incomes might deliver stronger, more resilient outcomes. ... Policymakers now face tough choices: continue supporting an industry that may never regain its pre-preference competitiveness without large subsidies, or begin designing and funding a phased transition that balances livelihoods protection with economic realities. Westpac’s review makes clear that without a planned roadmap and major capital injections for mechanisation and mill upgrades, the industry’s prospects will remain constrained.

headline: Labasa Mill kicks off the 2026 sugar season as first rail-delivered cane arrives and farmers await subsidy - FijiGlobalNews
summary_text: The 2026 sugar crushing season at the Fiji Sugar Corporation’s Labasa Mill officially opened on Wednesday, with the first 25 cane bins delivered by locomotive this afternoon, signaling the start of cane intake in Vanua Levu’s key milling centre. Mill staff and early suppliers were on site as rail trucks rolled in, marking the first rail-fed delivery of the new season. ... Among the earliest suppliers was Waiqele sector operator Satish Chand, who said dry conditions have created an “ideal window” for harvesting as much of the cane approaches maturity. “The weather is good, and it’s the best time to harvest. Things are going well on our side,” Chand told reporters, urging other farmers to make use of the favourable conditions now that crushing has begun. ... Despite the season’s start, Chand and other growers said many farmers remain cautious and are holding back on large-scale harvesting pending the release of the government’s cane planting subsidy. “I believe many farmers are still waiting for the subsidy, but we have to continue working because we need the income. We can’t let all the hard work we’ve put into our farms go to waste,” he added, explaining why some sectors are beginning only gradually. ... Activity at the mill this afternoon reflected that caution: only a handful of cane trucks were seen entering Labasa Mill and the usual parking area for queued trucks remained largely empty. Growers and industry observers are hoping that harvesting will pick up in the coming days as the crushing run gathers momentum, particularly in the Seaqaqa and Coqeloa sectors, which are being watched as potential next contributors to deliveries. ... The first rail delivery is notable against last year’s transport picture. In 2025 Labasa Mill closed its campaign after an extended run that began on June 17 and finished with 583,612 tonnes of cane crushed; road transport accounted for roughly 93 percent of deliveries and the rail system about seven percent. Mill operations and growers say timely harvesting and transport will be crucial this season to avoid the bottlenecks that forced extensions in previous years. ... As the Labasa campaign gets under way, the immediate indicators to watch are the pace of subsidy payments to farmers, an uptick in lorry movements to the mill and whether the rail system will be used more extensively for bulk deliveries. For now, growers such as Chand are encouraging colleagues to capitalise on the dry spell and begin harvesting, while many others wait for the government support they say is needed to scale up operations.

headline: Taxpayer-funded Australian sugar institute linked to abuses in West Papua
summary_text: ### Sugar Research Australia developed a sugarcane variety to grow in West Papua – months later, the UN accused Indonesian companies of displacing Indigenous peoples to make way for sugarcane production. ... A sugar research organisation funded by the Australian government is under scrutiny for its links to an Indonesian company allegedly involved in forcibly displacing Indigenous people and widespread deforestation in West Papua. ... In July 2024, Sugar Research Australia (SRA) – which received $9.4m in taxpayer money that year – agreed to supply six sugarcane varietals to Indonesian company, PT Global Papua Abadi (GPA). ... According to a December 2025 Greenpeace investigation, a consortium of ten Indonesian companies have so far been granted concessions for sugarcane cultivation covering 560,000 hectares in the Merauke region of West Papua, in what it described as “the world’s largest deforestation project”. ... Indigenous peoples in West Papua made formal objections to the sugar plantation development as early as June 2024. Since then, nine UN Special Rapporteurs have co-signed two letters to the Indonesian government alleging companies in the area have been forcibly displacing Indigenous people, first in October 2024 and again in March 2025. ... To produce 1.2m kilolitres of sugar, some additional 700,000 hectares will be carved out of the forest in Merauke – an area about three-fifths the size of Sydney and larger than the island of Bali. ... In the most recent letter from the UN, PT Global Papua Abadi and Pt Murni Nusantara Mandiri, itself a member of the GPA group, were alleged to have been allowed “to clear land, covering vast areas that overlap with the customary territories of these Indigenous tribes” with the assistance of the Indonesian military. ... The Indonesian government rejected these allegations, saying the development has been carried out in accordance with existing law and that “to date, no request has been submitted by any party for the area in question to be classified as customary land”. ... SRA’s transfer of the plant material appears to have enabled the aggressive development of sugarcane plantations across West Papua and in the district of Merauke since. ... In response to questions from Deepcut, an SRA spokesperson initially described the sugarcane varietals it provided as “genetically-modified”. SRA contacted Deepcut again after publication to say the original statement was incorrect, and the varietals were not genetically-modified. ... An SRA spokesperson said that the contract was “terminated in November 2024” with “no current or future intention of having any further involvement with the company in any capacity, commercially or otherwise”. But they did not clarify the circumstance under which the contract was ended, or whether the company retains rights to cultivate the crop. ... “SRA takes human rights and environmental issues seriously. SRA was not aware at the time of the engagement with PT GPA of the actions by both the Indonesian military and PT GPA in Merauke,” they told Deepcut. ... SRA’s involvement was raised by Greens Senator David Shoebridge and Coalition Senator Paul Scarr during a Senate committee hearing in late May. ... Scarr questioned why an Australian research institution had assisted Indonesian companies that were in direct competition with local producers but were not subject to similar environmental or human rights standards. ... Victoria Anderson, Secretary of the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Forestry (DAFF), stressed in the hearing that SRA was an independent organisation that “makes their own decisions” and has “their own accountable authority” separate to her department. ... Over the course of the hearing, Anderson was also asked to clarify her department’s understanding of the concurrent roles of Mark Day as non-executive director at SRA and the head of mills at GPA in 2024. Day later took up a full-time position with the Indonesian company. ... Day, a long-time figure in the Queensland and Indonesian sugar industry, previously served as CEO of Mackay Sugar, the head of Indonesian Sugar Estates and a former General Manager with CSR. ... Anderson said she was similarly unaware of the circumstances surrounding Day’s role, but said DAFF would investigate the matter further. ... An SRA spokesperson said “Mr Day himself had flagged early in the engagement that he would have a potential conflict of interest.” ... “To manage this, he was excluded from all board decisions and board papers regarding the engagement with PT GPA,” they said. ... “Mr Day was subsequently put on a leave of absence from the Board. He resigned from the Board in February 2024 as his ongoing dealings with the Indonesian sugar industry made it untenable for him to continue to serve as a director of SRA. Mr Day has not been involved with SRA since his resignation.” ... Speaking after the hearing, David Shoebridge said Indonesia’s activity in West Papua may be a difficult issue for Australia but there were “potentially very serious ramifications from this” and that “there needs to be political accountability”. ... “Australia can’t, on the one hand, openly cause further dispossession, further violence against West Papuans and on the other hand step away from the issue.”
