headline: Ingredion Tate & Lyle deal reshapes ingredients market
summary_text: ion Tate & Lyle deal resh ... The potential takeover of Tate & Lyle is part of a broader consolidation trend (Image: Getty/Klaus Vedfelt) ... ## The two ingredients giants could provide a one-stop shop for F&B and it’s part of a growing trend that will change the future of ingredients ... - The Ingredion–Tate & Lyle deal would create a major global ingredients supplier with broad solution capabilities - Over 75% of manufacturers prefer one-stop suppliers for efficiency and consistent reformulation outcomes - Sugar reduction is critical, with 98% of companies reformulating and needing multi-ingredient solutions - The combined company would strengthen its position in stevia, sucralose and emerging allulose - Industry consolidation is accelerating, putting pressure on mid-sized suppliers and reducing flexibility for manufacturers ... As pressure from consumers pushes for clean label products and GLP-1s turn many towards healthier, more intentional eating, food and beverage manufacturers are increasingly looking for integrated solutions for reformulation and innovation. That means ingredients suppliers will be vying to become the one-stop shop that they turn to. After agreeing a £2.7bn deal, the takeover of the UK’s Tate & Lyle by US ingredients giant Ingredion will go ahead if it passes scrutiny and the combination will be in a strong position to be a top one-stop shop. “A majority of manufacturers favour one-stop providers that offer both ingredients and complete solutions,” says Elizabeth Thundow, vice president of food and nutrition at B2B market insights and advisory firm, Kline and Company. “Over 75% prefer a single supplier for efficiency and consistency.” ... Add to this that 98% of F&B companies report a trend towards adopting blended solutions and 86% of F&B manufacturers seek closer collaboration with solutions providers and a clear picture is emerging. ... Sugar reduction is a key focus – 86% of F&B companies perceive sugar reduction as a necessity, according to Kline and Company’s manufacturer’s survey. And an extraordinary 98% are reformulating products to reduce sugar content. This would be a key strength for the Ingredion/Tate & Lyle combination. It will be able to address the problem of how sugar is replaced when it performs so many roles within a food or drink. “No single sweetener can replicate sugar’s full functionality,” explains Thundow. “Sugar’s multifunctional role (bulk, texture, stability) makes replacement technically challenging, often requiring multi-ingredient systems and process adjustments. “The combination [of Ingredion/Tate & Lyle] would create one of the most comprehensive sugar reduction portfolios globally, spanning stevia, sucralose, allulose, fibres, texturisers and stabilisers. This aligns with a structural shift in the market from single ingredients to multi-ingredients systems to integrated solutions partnerships.” ... Stevia continues to anchor the natural sweetener segment, benefiting from strong clean-label demand, according to Thundow. Ingredion’s stevia power was already bolstered by buying a majority stake in PureCircle in 2020. And now it’s here that the combination would hit its sweet spot. Kline analysis shows that the combined entity could account for 34% of global stevia sales in a market that is forecast to reach £1.3 billion by 2030. ... Meanwhile, says Thundow, sucralose remains a widely used synthetic option – Tate & Lyle revenue from sucralose alone was £260m in 2025. “Allulose is emerging as a high-growth, premium ingredient,” she adds. Stevia ... the natural sweetener ... (Luis Echeverri Urrea/Image: Getty/Luis Echeverri Urrea) ... Consolidation is part of a growing trend in the ingredients industry. “We have seen consolidation in ingredients over the past several years,” says Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at investment research company Morningstar. “Other notable transactions are IFF buying DuPont’s nutrition and biosciences business, the DSM-Firmenich merger and the Novozymes-Christian Hansen merger that created Novonesis. “Ingredient companies are constantly looking to add new products and categories to their portfolios to keep up with changing consumer preferences and accelerate volume growth. In many cases, a larger player will acquire smaller players as a way to add new product capabilities.” ... What does that mean for suppliers to the F&B industry? “IFF’s sale of its food ingredients business points in the same direction: companies making deliberate choices about where they compete, then building scale in those spaces,” says Filiberto Amati, advisor at FMCG consultancy Amati and Associates. “Mid-sized generalist suppliers are caught between large, integrated platforms and highly specialised niche players. That middle position is becoming hard to maintain.” ... “In a market where value is rapidly moving toward integrated sweetening systems, players focused on single ingredients risk being relegated to commoditised positions with margin pressure,” agrees Thundow. “Smaller or niche specialists may be forced to either differentiate in specific segments, such as rare sugars like allulose, or integrate into larger ecosystems. ... “Ultimately, this evolution points toward a future market structure dominated by fewer, larger ‘platform players’, where F&B manufacturers increasingly collaborate with multi-capability suppliers that can deliver end‑to‑end sugar-reduction solutions, rather than sourcing individual ingredients from a fragmented supplier base.” ... ## Potential downsides for F&B In the case of an Ingredion/Tate & Lyle combination, “a combined entity with about 15% global share of the global alternative sweeteners would become a top-tier supplier with stronger influence in key ingredients categories and solution systems”, says Thundow. “This scale enables greater negotiating leverage and higher switching costs, particularly as integrated systems become standard”. ... One-stop shops may also limit flexibility. “As integrated systems become more complex, switching suppliers becomes more difficult and resource intensive,” says Thundow. And innovation lock-in may also rear its head. “Proprietary systems may create dependency on specific formulations or platforms,” she says. Not all F&B companies will use one-stop shops. “Some still adopt multi-supplier strategies when greater customisation or access to specialised ingredients is required,” says Thundow. ... The future is looking like more M&A and this will have consequences for both brands and their suppliers. ... “Commodity sweeteners and starches, which are tied to indulgent, heavily processed formats, are under pressure especially as consumer seek clean eating,” says Ina Dawer, senior product manager for ingredients at global market intelligence firm, Euromonitor. “These categories are squeezed further by GLP-1 adoption and the backlash against ultra-processed foods, both of which push consumers toward nutrient density and ‘fewer but better’ calories. “For ingredients companies, the message is that scale alone no longer wins. Value is migrating to specialty and functional portfolios built around genuine health credentials. The market is moving from selling more calories to selling better calories and the winners will be the ones reading that shift at the ingredient level.” ... ? Sign up

headline: Australian rare sugars project targets high-value F&B sweetener opportunity
summary_text: - UQ researchers are using fermentation and “microbial cell factories” to produce low-calorie rare sugars from cane syrup. - The project could offer F&B manufacturers sugar alternatives with lower calories while retaining sweetness, texture, and baking performance. - The work, in partnership with MSF Sugar, positions rare sugars as a high-value opportunity for Australia’s sugar industry and is expected to run until 2027. ... Researchers in Australia are using fermentation to produce low-calorie rare sugars from cane syrup, which could potentially open a higher-value, healthier future for the country’s sugar industry. The approach could give F&B manufacturers an alternative to table sugar that delivers fewer calories while retaining the sweetness, texture, and baking performance consumers expect. ... Synthetic biologists and bioprocess engineers at The University of Queensland (UQ) are working on converting raw sugars into rare sugars in what they describe as “microbial cell factories” at the US$70 million UQ Biosustainability Hub. The project is housed at the hub, which was officially launched at the university’s St. Lucia campus today. ... Dr. Axayacatl Gonzalez, the Integrated Design Environment for Advanced biomanufacturing (IDEA) Bio manager and senior research platform fellow at the Australian Institute for Bioengineering and Nanotechnology, is leading the project along with his team at the hub, explains that rare sugars occur in some fruits, and they are increasingly coveted as alternative F&B sweeteners by the hospitality and commercial food industries. ... These sweeteners offer sensory and functional qualities to raw sugar while offering lower-calorie and health-focused benefits. However, he flags production costs as a barrier to their widespread applicability in the F&B sector. ... Consumer preferences are increasingly driving sweetener innovation, as nearly 72% actively cut sugar from their diets, suggests Innova Market Insights data. Soft drinks had the largest share of launches with sweeteners between Jul 2024 and Jun 2025, the market researcher highlights. ... Dr. Nathan Zhong engineered bacterial metabolism to create microbial cell factories that convert cane syrup feedstock into rare sugars. This demand is sharpening interest in production routes that can deliver sugar-like taste and functionality with fewer calories. At UQ, researchers are engineering bacteria commonly found in Queensland cane fields. However, they do not disclose the specific microbial strain used in the process. ... The ongoing project is a part of Australia’s AUD 370 million (US$264 million) Trailblazer Universities Program and is expected to run until 2027. ... Australia is one of the world’s largest sugar exporters, alongside Brazil, India, and Thailand, with the sector contributing around US$2 billion annually to the local economy, notes UQ. ... The scientists position rare sugars not only as a possible healthier sweetener for soft drinks and foods, but also as a high-value opportunity for Australia’s sugar industry to remain competitive in a changing global market. ... The UQ is collaborating with MSF Sugar, an Australian sugar grower, processor, marketer, and exporter of raw sugar, for the project. ... According to MSF Sugar’s general manager of business development, Jia Poontanasombat, rare sugars could ultimately help Australian sugar producers remain competitive internationally. ... The researchers emphasize that the project could help develop soft drinks and foods containing rare natural sugars with fewer calories but a similar taste to table sugar.“Rare sugars are a high-value commodity that possess obvious health and economic benefits,” she says. ... The launch of the Biosustainability Hub highlights the role of national research infrastructure in turning “breakthrough science into real-world products and economic value,” says Australia’s Federal Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill. ... He adds that the UQ Biosustainability Hub houses two National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS)-funded national research facilities, offering researchers and industry the tools needed to rapidly develop and scale new biosolutions. ... “Through NCRIS, the Government is not only supporting cutting-edge facilities and ‘kit’, but also the expertise needed to translate data into real-world outcomes. This is about ensuring Australia remains globally competitive, while building a more productive, resilient and forward-looking economy now and for the next generation,” Hill concludes.

headline: Fiji sugar stocks near depletion by end of June unless mills start crushing next week - FijiGlobalNews
summary_text: Fiji faces the prospect of running out of sugar for local sale by the end of this month unless mills start crushing as scheduled next week, Fiji Sugar Corporation chief executive Bhan Pratap Singh warned this week, laying bare a sector squeezed by last season’s record-low cane yields, ageing plant and rising operating costs. ... “We will be running out of sugar soon. By the end of this month, there will be no more sugar available to sell locally if the mills do not start,” Singh told reporters as he urged all three sugar mills to commence operations next week. His comments came as he answered questions before the Standing Committee on Economic Affairs about FSC’s 2024 and 2025 annual reports. ... The urgency is immediate. Singh said the delayed start of the Lautoka mill has already affected operations and any further postponement could create significant challenges for both domestic supplies and export commitments. To preserve stocks at home, FSC has already reduced sugar sales to Pacific Island countries and prioritised the domestic market until milling resumes. ... The squeeze on supply is rooted in last year’s severe decline in cane production. FSC recorded its lowest-ever cane production during the 2025 crushing season, Singh told the committee. In 2025 the mills crushed just over 1.33 million tonnes of cane and produced 126,500 tonnes of sugar, down from 1.57 million tonnes of cane and 139,628 tonnes of sugar in 2024. Average cane yield fell to 46.4 tonnes per hectare, Singh said. ... Low and falling production is exacerbating other problems. Singh pointed to ageing plant and equipment, underutilised machinery and market volatility as drivers of very high operating costs. With less cane to process, fixed costs are spread over smaller volumes and the mills run less efficiently. ... The supply crunch also complicates export obligations. Singh highlighted a preferential shipment to the United States, with an annual quota estimated between 9,000 and 10,000 metric tonnes that brings a higher return than some other markets. But with local stocks dwindling, FSC has had to rebalance where it sells sugar. ... Farmers say the industry’s economics are deteriorating. Growers have protested falling returns while production costs—particularly for harvesting and delivery—have climbed. A forecast cane price announced by the Sugar Industry Tribunal under the Master Award was set at $57.40 per tonne, a figure many growers argued would not cover rising input and labour costs. ... The Sugar Industry Ministry moved to blunt the fallout, and after consultations announced a guaranteed price for the 2026 crop season of $85 per tonne. The $85 figure comprises the Tribunal’s $57.40 forecast plus a government top-up intended to reflect higher farming costs. ... Those local cost pressures feed into the broader agricultural economy. Lower cane yields and the risk of growers reducing area under cane would further strain milling throughput and perpetuate the operating-cost cycle Singh described. FSC’s plea to begin crushing next week is therefore both an operational appeal and a call to stabilise supply chains before shortages deepen. ... Singh’s appearance before the committee also reiterated the structural challenge FSC faces: unlike earlier eras when part of Fiji’s sugar was sold under a preferential EU protocol, all sugar produced by FSC is now sold on the open market. That exposes the company to price swings that complicate planning for growers and millers alike. ... Operationally, the mills are sensitive to the timing of the crush. Delays to the start reduce the season’s available milling days, compressing operations and increasing the risk of cane deterioration in the fields. Singh warned that the delayed Lautoka start had already disrupted planned schedules; he urged that all three mills open next week “as scheduled” to avoid compounding the problem. ... Government involvement in the sector remains active. The ministry’s decision to top up the forecast price to $85 per tonne is aimed at keeping farmers on the land and offsetting immediate cost pressures, but it does not resolve the longer-term issues Singh flagged: drought-affected yields, ageing infrastructure and the commercial realities of open-market sugar sales. ... Singh and Dutt both emphasised engagement through formal channels. Dutt said farmers’ concerns had been raised and addressed through industry consultations; Singh framed his call for a timely start to milling as a practical measure to protect local supply and meet export commitments. ... The sector now waits to see whether the mills will meet the proposed start dates. If they do, farmers and mill workers will be watching yields and factory performance closely. If not, Singh’s warning that local outlets could run dry by month’s end will become a reality with immediate consequences for consumers and exporters alike.

headline: Gold Coast canefarmers 'devastated' after sugar mill terminates contract
summary_text: Rocky Point Sugar Mill on Queensland’s Gold Coast will stop crushing cane after the 2027 season, putting around 50 growers’ longer-term supply arrangements at risk. Industry stakeholders are examining whether cane could instead be transported approximately 100 kilometres to Condong Sugar Mill in northern New South Wales. The development highlights ongoing consolidation and logistical vulnerability in Australia’s regional sugar-milling network.

headline: STL assumes operation of Queensland sugar terminals
summary_text: Sugar Terminals Limited formally assumed ownership and operation of Queensland’s six bulk sugar export terminals from 1 July: Cairns, Mourilyan, Lucinda, Townsville, Mackay and Bundaberg. The change places STL in charge of operating key export gateways and is intended to support safe, efficient and fair terminal management. For procurement and logistics managers, the transition is significant because it affects the infrastructure handling Queensland’s bulk sugar flows.

headline: Global ransomware group reportedly claim cyber attack that shut down Mackay Sugar mills
summary_text: A Russian-speaking ransomware group reportedly claimed responsibility for a cyberattack that disrupted Mackay Sugar’s Farleigh and Racecourse mills in Queensland. The incident halted harvesting activities for many of the approximately 1,300 farms supplying the company, while the mills conducted manual crushing and steam testing before a phased restart. The disruption demonstrates the exposure of sugar production, cane logistics and grower payments or supply coordination to operational technology and cyber risks.

headline: Australian rare sugars project targets high-value F&B sweetener opportunity
summary_text: University of Queensland researchers and MSF Sugar are developing fermentation-based microbial cell factories to convert cane syrup into low-calorie rare sugars. The project aims to produce sweeteners that retain sugar-like sweetness, texture and baking performance while creating a higher-value outlet for Australia’s sugar industry. Supported through Australia’s Trailblazer Universities Program, the research is expected to continue through 2027.

headline: Mackay Sugar mills shut by cyber attack hope to reopen next week
summary_text: Mackay Sugar shut two of its three Queensland mills after discovering compromised operating systems and planned a staged restart. Farleigh Mill resumed limited manual crushing to process already-cut cane before sugar content deteriorated, but cane supply and logistics systems remained under restoration and additional cane was temporarily not accepted. Mackay Sugar, Australia’s second-largest raw sugar producer, said it was working with cybersecurity specialists and authorities.

headline: Sugarcane industry to plan for future as worries about urban sprawl grow
summary_text: Sugarcane growers near Cairns are seeking stronger protection for agricultural land as urban expansion reduces available farmland and threatens the region’s production base. Industry groups and other stakeholders are forming a committee to influence future town-planning decisions. The issue adds a structural supply risk for North Queensland’s sugar industry, which has already experienced mill closures and declining cane production in parts of Far North Queensland.
